Put it into practice
docs.text:
Create your first product roadmap using the insights you've gathered during customer discovery and SME interviews.

Start with your research, not a list of features.

Review your interview notes and identify three to five important customer problems or opportunities.

For each one:

  1. Identify: Describe the problem in the customer's terms.
  2. Support: Record the interviews or other evidence that helped you identify it.
  3. Understand: Explain why the problem matters and who experiences it.
  4. Define: Describe the outcome you'd like to help customers achieve.
  5. Prioritize: Decide whether the opportunity belongs in your Now, Next, or Later category.

Use Miro or another tool you're comfortable with to organize your roadmap visually.

Your initial roadmap might look like this:

Priority Customer problem Desired outcome What we need to learn Now Customers spend too much time preparing reports Reduce manual reporting effort Which steps create the most difficulty? Next Customers struggle to find information Make important information easier to access How do customers currently organize their records? Later Customers want better visibility into performance Help customers understand important business information Which information matters most to their decisions?

These are illustrative examples. Your roadmap should reflect what you've learned from your own research.

Before considering your first roadmap ready, ask yourself:

  • Can I explain where each priority came from?
  • Does my roadmap reflect real customer problems rather than only my own ideas?
  • Have I considered relevant insights from subject-matter experts?
  • Am I clear about which findings are supported by evidence and which are still assumptions?
  • Have I identified the outcomes I want to achieve?
  • Do I know what needs to be investigated or tested next?
  • Is the roadmap flexible enough to change as I learn?

Your first roadmap doesn't need to be detailed or permanent.

It should help you organize what you've learned, communicate your priorities, and decide where to focus your attention.

Consider reviewing your roadmap with your TechAlliance advisor to discuss your priorities, assumptions, and next steps.

As you move into the Validation stage, you'll use your roadmap to guide the development and testing of potential solutions.

The goal is to build something that addresses a meaningful customer problem, not simply to complete a list of planned features.

docs.title: Learn from people who understand your industry
docs.text:
When exploring a business idea, you don't need to figure everything out on your own.

People with experience in your industry, technology, or target market can help you understand challenges, identify important considerations, and explore questions you may not have thought to ask.

A subject-matter expert (SME) is someone with specialized knowledge or practical experience in a particular field.

This could be an industry professional, technical specialist, researcher, regulatory advisor, experienced entrepreneur, or someone who has worked extensively with the type of problem you're investigating.

Interviewing these experts can help you develop a better understanding of the environment in which your business might operate.

SME interviews are optional, but highly recommended. They can provide valuable context alongside your customer discovery research, particularly when you're entering an unfamiliar, technical, or regulated market.

docs.title: Why speak with subject-matter experts?
docs.text:
Customer discovery helps you understand how potential customers experience a problem.

SME interviews help you understand the broader context surrounding that problem.

For example, if you're developing a solution for healthcare organizations, conversations with healthcare professionals, technology specialists, and people familiar with relevant regulations may reveal considerations that aren't immediately obvious from customer interviews alone.

SME interviews can help you:

  • Understand your industry: Learn how the market operates, who participates in it, and what influences decisions.
  • Explore technical considerations: Identify potential requirements, limitations, or challenges related to your proposed approach.
  • Understand regulations and standards: Learn which rules, certifications, or industry practices may be relevant to your business.
  • Identify existing solutions: Discover established approaches, emerging technologies, or alternatives you haven't considered.
  • Challenge assumptions: Hear informed perspectives that may differ from your initial understanding.
  • Identify opportunities: Explore gaps, changes, or emerging needs that may deserve further investigation.
  • Build connections: Meet people who may introduce you to additional experts, industry contacts, or potential customers.

You don't need to become an expert in every area of your business.

The goal is to learn enough to make better decisions, recognize important risks, and identify where additional research or specialized advice may be needed.

docs.title: SME interviews are not a replacement for customer discovery
docs.text:
An industry expert may understand a market extremely well without experiencing the same challenges as your target customers.

They may also have opinions about what customers need that don't fully reflect how those customers behave.

For this reason, it's important to distinguish between:

  • Customer evidence: What potential customers say about their own experiences, supported by specific examples and behaviours.
  • Expert insight: What knowledgeable professionals explain about industry practices, trends, constraints, and possible opportunities.

Both can inform your understanding, but they answer different questions.

For example, an expert might explain why a particular process is inefficient across an industry.

Customer interviews can help you understand whether the people performing that process recognize the inefficiency as a significant problem and what they're doing about it.

Use expert insights to inform your research, not to replace direct evidence from potential customers.

docs.title: Who should you interview?
docs.text:
The most relevant experts will depend on your business idea and the questions you're trying to answer.

Consider speaking with:

  • Industry professionals: People with experience working in the market you want to enter.
  • Technical specialists: Professionals who understand the technologies, systems, or processes involved in your idea.
  • Researchers and academics: People studying relevant scientific, technical, economic, or social topics.
  • Regulatory and compliance specialists: Professionals familiar with applicable laws, standards, or industry requirements.
  • Experienced entrepreneurs: Founders or business leaders who have worked in similar markets.
  • Supply chain and distribution specialists: People who understand how products and services reach customers.
  • Industry advisors and consultants: Professionals who work with organizations facing challenges similar to those you're investigating.

You may find relevant experts through professional associations, universities, research institutions, industry events, LinkedIn, and introductions from your existing network.

Consider asking your TechAlliance advisor whether they can help you identify relevant expertise or connections.

Start with the knowledge gaps that matter most to your business rather than trying to interview every possible type of expert.

docs.title: How to conduct an SME interview
docs.text: An effective SME interview requires preparation, curiosity, and a willingness to explore unexpected insights.

docs.title: 1. Define what you want to learn
docs.text:
Before contacting an expert, identify the questions you hope they can help answer.

For example:

  • What are the main challenges facing this industry?
  • How is a particular process typically managed?
  • What technical or regulatory requirements should I understand?
  • What common mistakes do new businesses make in this market?

Choose experts whose experience is relevant to those questions.

docs.title: 2. Research the expert and the topic
docs.text:
Learn about the expert's background, professional experience, and area of specialization.

Review relevant industry information before the conversation so you can move beyond basic questions.

You don't need to know everything, but preparation helps you make better use of the expert's time.

docs.title: 3. Prepare thoughtful questions
docs.text:
Develop an interview guide with open-ended questions.

Avoid asking only for general opinions about your business idea.

Instead, encourage experts to share specific examples, explain industry practices, and describe challenges they've encountered.

docs.title: 4. Explain the purpose of the conversation
docs.text:
Briefly introduce your venture and explain what you're trying to learn.

Make it clear that you're seeking their perspective and experience.

Be respectful of their time, particularly when someone is sharing specialized knowledge without compensation.

If you want to record the conversation, ask for permission first.

docs.title: 5. Follow interesting insights
docs.text:
Use your prepared questions as a guide, but don't be afraid to explore unexpected topics.

If an expert mentions an unfamiliar challenge or surprising trend, ask them to explain further.

Questions such as "Can you give me an example?" or "Why does that happen?" can help you move beyond general observations.

docs.title: 6. Summarize and clarify
docs.text:
Before ending the interview, briefly summarize what you've learned and check that you've understood the expert correctly.

Ask whether there are important considerations you haven't discussed.

You can also ask whether they recommend additional resources or other people who might offer a useful perspective.

docs.title: 7. Document your findings
docs.text:
Review your notes soon after the conversation.

Record important insights, examples, recommended resources, and questions that need further investigation.

Distinguish between established facts, the expert's professional opinions, and your own interpretations.

docs.title: SME interview guide
docs.text:
Use these questions as a starting point when preparing to speak with a subject-matter expert.

Choose the questions most relevant to the expert's experience and your business idea.

Understanding the industry

  • Can you tell me about your experience in this field?
  • What are some of the biggest challenges facing this industry?
  • How have these challenges changed over time?
  • What trends or developments do you think are important to understand?

Exploring the problem

  • How is [SPECIFIC PROBLEM OR PROCESS] typically handled today?
  • What makes this problem difficult to address?
  • Which organizations or groups are most affected?
  • What approaches have you seen work well or poorly?
  • Can you share an example from your experience?

Understanding constraints

  • What technical requirements should someone entering this market understand?
  • Are there regulations, standards, or certifications that may apply?
  • What barriers make it difficult for new solutions to enter the market?
  • What common mistakes do new businesses make in this area?

Exploring opportunities

  • Where do you see gaps or unmet needs in the market?
  • Are there changes that could create new opportunities?
  • What existing solutions or organizations should I investigate?
  • What assumptions about this market would you encourage me to question?

Closing the conversation

  • What important questions haven't I asked?
  • Are there resources you recommend reviewing?
  • Is there someone else whose perspective would be valuable?
  • Would you be open to a follow-up question if something comes up during my research?

You don't need to cover every topic in one interview.

Focus on the expert's area of knowledge and ask follow-up questions when something deserves further exploration.

docs.title: SME interview notes template
docs.text:
Use a consistent format to document your conversations.

Category Notes Interview date Expert's field or specialization Main questions investigated Important industry insights Technical or regulatory considerations Existing solutions or approaches Risks or barriers identified Potential opportunities Recommended resources or contacts Assumptions supported or challenged Questions requiring further research

Keep the information organized so you can compare insights across different interviews.

Avoid collecting or sharing confidential information without appropriate permission.

docs.title: Assumption and evidence tracker
docs.text:
SME interviews can help you identify assumptions that need further investigation.

Create a simple table to track what you've learned.

Assumption Expert insight Supporting evidence Next step Assumption A Assumption B Assumption C

For each assumption, consider:

  • Did the expert support or challenge it?
  • Was their response based on direct experience, research, or professional opinion?
  • Are there credible sources that support the insight?
  • Should you investigate it with additional experts or potential customers?

This helps you avoid treating one person's opinion as a confirmed fact.

docs.title: LinkedIn
docs.text:
LinkedIn can help you identify professionals with experience in your target industry or area of research.

Search for people by role, industry, organization, or area of specialization.

Review their backgrounds before reaching out and explain clearly why you'd value their perspective.

docs.title: Google Scholar
docs.text:
Google Scholar is a search tool for academic publications and research.

You can use it to find relevant studies, identify researchers working in your field, and explore technical or scientific information related to your idea.

When reviewing research, consider its publication date, methodology, and relevance to your specific question.

docs.title: Calendly
docs.text:
Calendly is a scheduling platform that can help you coordinate interviews with experts.

Sharing your availability can make it easier to arrange conversations with busy professionals.

docs.title: Google Meet
docs.text:
Google Meet is a video meeting platform you can use to conduct remote SME interviews.

It can help you connect with experts outside your immediate geographic area.

If you plan to record an interview, obtain the participant's permission and review the available recording and privacy settings.

docs.title: Google Docs
docs.text:
Google Docs can help you prepare interview questions, organize notes, and summarize findings.

Consider keeping a separate document for each interview and maintaining a shared summary of important insights.

Store your notes securely and limit access when they contain confidential or sensitive information.

docs.title: Velocity Partners - How to get the most out of SME interviews
docs.text: This article focuses on interviewing subject-matter experts for B2B content development. Its guidance on preparation, thoughtful questions, active listening, and following up on interesting insights can also help founders conduct more useful expert interviews.

docs.title: Put it into practice
docs.text:
Optional but highly recommended: Conduct one or two SME interviews to strengthen your understanding of the problem, industry, or market you're exploring.

You don't need to complete this exercise before continuing with customer discovery. Consider it an additional opportunity to challenge assumptions and identify information you may have overlooked.

Start by identifying an important knowledge gap.

For example:

  • I don't fully understand how this industry operates.
  • I'm unsure which technical requirements might apply.
  • I need to learn more about relevant regulations.
  • I want to understand why existing solutions work the way they do.
  • I need an experienced perspective on a problem I've identified.

Then:

  1. Identify: Find one or two people with relevant expertise.
  2. Prepare: Research their background and develop a short list of questions.
  3. Connect: Reach out with a clear explanation of what you're researching and why their experience would be valuable.
  4. Interview: Ask open-ended questions, listen carefully, and explore specific examples.
  5. Document: Record important insights, assumptions, and recommended resources.
  6. Reflect: Decide what you've learned and what needs further investigation.

After your conversations, ask yourself:

  • What did I learn that I didn't know before?
  • Did the experts challenge any of my assumptions?
  • What industry, technical, or regulatory considerations should I investigate further?
  • Were there differences between the experts' perspectives?
  • What information still needs to be verified?
  • How might these insights influence my customer discovery interviews?

Summarize the most useful findings and identify any next steps.

Consider sharing your insights with your TechAlliance advisor to discuss how they relate to your business idea and customer research.

Remember: Expert interviews can strengthen your understanding of the market, but they don't replace speaking directly with potential customers.

Use both perspectives to develop a clearer picture of the problem you're exploring.

docs.title: Build the foundations for a stronger business
docs.text:
You've explored your opportunity, investigated the problem, and started testing your solution. Now it's time to focus on the foundations that will help you turn that solution into a business that can operate effectively and grow.

The Efficiency stage helps you think through the practical aspects of running your business, from managing finances and organizing operations to developing processes and making the most of your resources.

You don't need to have everything figured out from the start. This is your opportunity to build the structure, habits, and systems that will support your business as it develops.

docs.title: What you'll explore
docs.text:
The resources in this section can help you:

  • Develop your business model: Explore how your business will create, deliver, and capture value.
  • Plan your finances: Understand costs, revenue, pricing, cash flow, and the financial decisions involved in running your business.
  • Build your operations: Explore the processes, tools, and systems needed to deliver your solution and manage day-to-day activities.
  • Manage your resources: Consider how to use your time, budget, technology, and available expertise effectively.
  • Establish your business foundations: Learn about important considerations such as business structure, legal requirements, contracts, and other administrative responsibilities.
  • Prepare your team: Explore roles, responsibilities, and approaches to building a team that supports your business goals.

docs.title: How to use these resources
docs.text:
Explore the topics available in this section to understand the different elements involved in building and operating your business.

Each topic may include practical notes, tools, templates, or links to additional reading that can help you plan your operations, organize your resources, and make informed business decisions.

If your TechAlliance advisor has recommended specific resources, start there. You can return to other topics as your business needs and priorities evolve.

docs.title: Questions to consider
docs.text:
As you build your business foundations, think about:

  • How will my business generate revenue and manage its costs?
  • What processes and systems do I need to deliver my solution consistently?
  • What legal, financial, and administrative responsibilities should I understand?
  • How can I make better use of my time, budget, and other resources?
  • What skills, roles, or external expertise will my business need?
  • What challenges could affect my ability to operate effectively as demand grows?

Use these questions to identify gaps in your business foundations, prioritize improvements, and prepare for conversations with your TechAlliance advisor.

docs.title: Your next step
docs.text:
Start with the topic that addresses an important operational or business challenge you're currently facing.

Use what you learn to strengthen your business foundations, improve how you work, and prepare for the opportunities and challenges of the Scale stage.

docs.title: Know when money comes in, when it goes out, and how long it will last
docs.text:
You've developed your sales process, defined your operating needs, and started planning the resources required to grow your business.

Now it's time to understand what those plans mean for your cash.

A cash flow forecast estimates how much money your business expects to receive and spend over a defined period.

It helps you understand whether you'll have enough cash to pay your bills, support your operations, and make planned investments.

A cash flow forecast can help you answer questions such as:

  • How much cash do we have available today?
  • When do we expect customers to pay us?
  • How much will it cost to operate each month?
  • Can we afford our planned hires and investments?
  • What happens if sales are lower than expected?
  • When might we run short of cash?
  • How much additional funding might we need, and when?

A business can generate revenue and still run out of cash.

For example, imagine your company signs a $20,000 contract in January, but the customer won't pay until March.

Meanwhile, you need to pay employees, software subscriptions, and suppliers in January and February.

Even though you've made a sale, you still need enough cash to cover those expenses before the payment arrives.

Your cash flow forecast helps you see these gaps before they become problems.

docs.title: Understand cash flow, revenue, and profit
docs.text:
These terms are connected, but they mean different things.

Revenue is the income your business earns from selling products or services.

Profit is what remains after subtracting the expenses associated with generating that revenue, according to the accounting method used.

Cash flow tracks the actual movement of money into and out of your business.

For example:

You invoice a customer for $5,000 in January.

The customer pays in March.

Depending on your accounting method, you may recognize the revenue before March. However, the cash doesn't enter your bank account until the customer pays.

Similarly, you might purchase equipment in one month even though its cost is recognized over a longer period in your financial statements.

Your cash flow forecast focuses on when money is actually received or paid.

It isn't a replacement for bookkeeping, an income statement, or other financial reports.

It's a planning tool that helps you understand your future cash position.

docs.title: Start with the information you've already collected
docs.text:
You don't need to begin your forecast from scratch.

Much of the information should come from the work you've completed throughout the Knowledge Hub.

docs.title: Sales assets and process
docs.text:
Your sales planning provides assumptions about:

  • Expected customer acquisition
  • Average sale value
  • Sales targets
  • Sales cycle length
  • Pricing
  • Customer payment terms
  • Recurring or repeat purchases

Use these assumptions to estimate future customer payments.

Remember that a sales target isn't guaranteed revenue, and expected revenue isn't necessarily cash collected in the same month.

docs.title: Ops & HR plan
docs.text:
Your operations plan provides information about:

  • Current operating expenses
  • Salaries and employer-related costs
  • Contractor fees
  • Software and infrastructure
  • Equipment purchases
  • Hiring plans
  • Capacity limits
  • Growth-related investments

Use these estimates to forecast when your business will need to spend money.

Pay particular attention to costs that must be paid before additional sales can be delivered.

docs.title: MVP and pilot results
docs.text:
Your Validation-stage work may provide early evidence about:

  • What customers are willing to pay
  • How often they purchase or use your offering
  • The cost of delivering the product or service
  • How long onboarding takes
  • Customer support requirements
  • Whether customers continue after an initial purchase

Use actual results where available.

If you're still making assumptions, document them clearly.

docs.title: Choose a practical forecasting period
docs.text:
For most early-stage startups, a 12-month forecast organized by month is a useful starting point.

It provides enough visibility to plan operating expenses, customer payments, and upcoming investments without requiring an overly complex model.

If you're preparing a funding application or planning major investments, you may need to forecast 24 months or longer.

Some businesses also benefit from a short-term weekly forecast, particularly when cash is tight or large payments are approaching.

For example:

  • Weekly forecast: Helps manage immediate payment obligations and short-term cash availability.
  • Monthly forecast: Helps plan operating costs, hiring, investments, and funding needs.
  • Longer-term forecast: Helps evaluate growth scenarios and future capital requirements.

Start with the level of detail your business needs.

A simple forecast that you regularly update is more useful than a complicated model that becomes outdated.

docs.title: Estimate your cash inflows
docs.text:
Cash inflows are the amounts of money you expect to receive.

Depending on your business, they may include:

  • Customer payments
  • Subscription payments
  • Deposits and advance payments
  • Grants or contributions
  • Loans
  • Equity investments
  • Other cash receipts

Separate cash generated by business operations from money received through financing.

This helps you understand whether the business can support itself through customer revenue or currently depends on outside capital.

docs.title: Estimate customer payments
docs.text:
Start with your sales forecast.

For each product or service, consider:

  • How many sales do you expect?
  • What will customers pay?
  • When will the sale occur?
  • When will the customer actually pay?
  • Will the payment be received all at once or in instalments?

For example:

Month Expected sales Expected cash collected January $10,000 $4,000 February $15,000 $9,000 March $20,000 $17,000

These figures are illustrative.

The difference between sales and collections could result from payment terms, deposits, or invoices that haven't been paid yet.

Use your actual payment terms and customer behaviour wherever possible.

docs.title: Be careful with uncertain funding
docs.text:
If you're applying for a grant, loan, or investment, don't automatically treat the funding as guaranteed.

Record the expected amount, potential timing, and current status.

Consider preparing a scenario that excludes funding you haven't secured.

This will help you understand whether your business can continue operating if the money arrives later than expected or doesn't arrive.

docs.title: Estimate your cash outflows
docs.text:
Cash outflows are the payments your business expects to make.

Start with your Ops & HR plan and list the expenses required to operate.

docs.title: Fixed and recurring expenses
docs.text:
These may include:

  • Salaries and payroll-related costs
  • Rent
  • Insurance
  • Software subscriptions
  • Internet and communications
  • Accounting and professional services
  • Regular loan payments

Some expenses may be paid monthly, while others are quarterly or annually.

Record them in the months when payment is expected.

docs.title: Variable expenses
docs.text:
These change with your sales volume or level of activity.

Examples include:

  • Materials and inventory
  • Manufacturing
  • Shipping
  • Payment processing fees
  • Usage-based software or hosting
  • Contractors paid per project
  • Sales commissions

Use your expected sales and delivery volume to estimate these costs.

For example, if each product costs $40 to manufacture and you expect to produce 100 units, your estimated manufacturing cost would be $4,000.

However, you also need to consider when you'll pay for the materials or production.

docs.title: One-time investments
docs.text:
These may include:

  • Equipment purchases
  • Website or software development
  • Office setup
  • Initial inventory
  • Professional services
  • Recruitment and onboarding expenses
  • New infrastructure

Use the timing established in your Ops & HR growth plan.

docs.title: Taxes and other obligations
docs.text:
Consider applicable tax payments, payroll remittances, loan repayments, and other financial obligations.

For Canadian businesses, GST/HST collection and remittance may affect cash timing.

Amounts collected on behalf of tax authorities shouldn't be treated as unrestricted operating cash.

Tax treatment and remittance requirements depend on your circumstances. Consult a qualified accountant or relevant government guidance when preparing these estimates.

docs.title: Build your monthly cash flow forecast
docs.text:
Once you've estimated inflows and outflows, organize them into a spreadsheet.

A basic forecast follows this structure:

Opening cash balance + Cash inflows - Cash outflows = Closing cash balance

The closing balance from one month becomes the opening balance for the next.

For example:

Category January February March Opening cash balance $25,000 $21,000 $17,000 Customer payments $8,000 $12,000 $16,000 Other cash inflows $0 $0 $0 Total cash inflows $8,000 $12,000 $16,000 Operating payments $10,000 $13,000 $14,000 Equipment purchases $2,000 $3,000 $0 Total cash outflows $12,000 $16,000 $14,000 Net cash flow -$4,000 -$4,000 $2,000 Closing cash balance $21,000 $17,000 $19,000

In this example, the business spends more than it receives in January and February.

Its cash balance begins to recover in March.

However, the business still needs to understand whether its available cash will be sufficient to support future expenses and growth.

docs.title: Check the lowest projected cash balance
docs.text:
Don't focus only on your cash position at the end of the year.

Look at each month to identify when cash is expected to be lowest.

For businesses with significant payments occurring within a month, a monthly forecast may hide short-term shortages.

If necessary, create a weekly forecast for periods when cash availability is particularly important.

docs.title: Understand your burn rate and runway
docs.text: Two useful financial measures for startups are burn rate and cash runway.

docs.title: Burn rate
docs.text:
Burn rate describes how quickly your business is using cash.

Gross burn generally refers to total cash operating outflows during a period.

Net burn refers to the amount of cash your business consumes after accounting for operating cash inflows.

For example:

If your business spends $15,000 per month and receives $8,000 from customers, its net operating cash burn is $7,000 per month.

If operating cash inflows exceed operating outflows, the business may be generating cash rather than burning it.

Be consistent about which cash flows you include in your calculations.

docs.title: Cash runway
docs.text:
Cash runway estimates how long your available cash can support your business if it continues consuming cash.

A simple estimate is:

Cash runway = Available cash ÷ Average monthly net burn

For example:

If you have $42,000 in available cash and your net burn is $7,000 per month, your estimated runway is six months.

However, this calculation assumes your burn rate remains constant.

In reality, customer payments, hiring, equipment purchases, and other expenses may change significantly.

Use your month-by-month forecast to identify when cash could run out rather than relying only on a simple runway calculation.

docs.title: Prepare different financial scenarios
docs.text:
Your forecast is based on assumptions about future events.

Some of those assumptions will be wrong.

Instead of relying on a single projection, prepare a few scenarios to understand how different outcomes could affect your business.

docs.title: Base scenario
docs.text:
Your most reasonable estimate based on current evidence and operating plans.

It might assume:

  • Sales develop according to your current forecast.
  • Customers pay according to expected terms.
  • Planned expenses occur on schedule.
  • Hiring follows your Ops & HR plan.

docs.title: Conservative scenario
docs.text:
A scenario where important assumptions don't work out as expected.

For example:

  • Sales are lower than anticipated.
  • Customers take longer to pay.
  • A major contract is delayed.
  • Operating expenses increase.
  • Planned funding arrives later than expected.

This scenario helps you identify risks and prepare responses before cash becomes tight.

docs.title: Growth scenario
docs.text:
A scenario where demand increases faster than expected.

For example:

  • More customers purchase your offering.
  • Revenue grows faster than planned.
  • You need additional employees sooner.
  • Production or infrastructure costs increase.
  • You must invest before receiving all the additional customer payments.

Faster growth doesn't always improve your immediate cash position.

It may create additional working capital needs.

docs.title: Compare the results
docs.text:
For each scenario, review:

  • Lowest projected cash balance
  • Months with negative net cash flow
  • Expected runway
  • Hiring and investment requirements
  • Potential funding gaps
  • Decisions you may need to make

Don't choose arbitrary growth percentages and treat them as reliable forecasts.

Use actual sales evidence, operating constraints, and reasonable assumptions.

docs.title: Identify potential funding gaps
docs.text:
One of the most important outcomes of your forecast is understanding when your business might need additional capital.

A funding gap occurs when the cash available to your business is insufficient to cover planned payments and maintain an appropriate operating buffer.

For example, your forecast might show that:

  • You have enough cash to operate for the next four months.
  • A planned equipment purchase will reduce your cash balance significantly.
  • Customer payments aren't expected to increase until several months later.
  • You may need additional funding before making that investment.

This information gives you time to evaluate your options.

Depending on your circumstances, those options might include:

  • Adjusting the timing of an investment
  • Reducing or postponing discretionary expenses
  • Improving customer payment collection
  • Revisiting payment terms
  • Changing your growth plan
  • Exploring financing or investment opportunities

Avoid assuming that outside funding will arrive exactly when needed.

Loans, grants, and investments can involve application processes, approvals, negotiations, and delays.

Your forecast should help you identify when to begin exploring funding, not just when your bank balance is approaching zero.

docs.title: Review actual results and update your forecast
docs.text:
Your first cash flow forecast won't be perfectly accurate.

That's expected.

Its value comes from using it regularly to understand your business and improve your decisions.

At the end of each month:

  1. Record the cash you actually received.
  2. Record the payments you actually made.
  3. Compare the results with your forecast.
  4. Identify the largest differences.
  5. Investigate why those differences occurred.
  6. Update your assumptions for the months ahead.

For example, if customers consistently take 45 days to pay instead of the 30 days you expected, adjust your future cash collection assumptions.

If your hosting costs increase faster than expected, update your operating expense forecast.

If you delay a planned hire, adjust the timing of the related costs.

docs.title: Distinguish timing differences from ongoing changes
docs.text:
Not every difference between forecast and actual results indicates a problem with your business model.

A payment arriving one month late may be a timing difference.

A recurring pattern of customers paying later than expected may require a change to your assumptions or collection process.

Similarly, a one-time equipment purchase is different from an ongoing increase in monthly operating costs.

Understanding the cause helps you make better decisions.

Your forecast should evolve as you learn more about how your business actually operates.

docs.title: Monthly cash flow forecast
docs.text:
Use a spreadsheet with one column for each month.

Organize it into five main sections:

1. Opening cash balance

The cash available at the beginning of the month.

2. Cash inflows

Customer payments, financing received, and other cash receipts.

3. Cash outflows

Operating expenses, payroll, supplier payments, equipment purchases, taxes, debt payments, and other cash payments.

4. Net cash flow

Total cash inflows minus total cash outflows.

5. Closing cash balance

Opening cash balance plus net cash flow.

Extend the forecast for at least 12 months, or longer if required for your planning or funding application.

docs.title: Put it into practice
docs.text:
Create a cash flow forecast that shows how your business expects to receive and spend money over the coming months.

By the end of this exercise, you should understand your projected cash position, the assumptions behind it, and when you may need additional funding or changes to your operating plan.

Start by gathering your sales projections, Ops & HR plan, current financial records, and planned investments.

Then:

  1. Choose your forecasting period. Start with 12 months of monthly projections, or use a longer period if required for funding or business planning.
  2. Record your opening cash balance. Use the actual cash available to the business at the beginning of the forecast.
  3. Estimate customer payments. Use your sales plan, pricing, expected sales volume, and payment terms to project when cash will be collected.
  4. Identify other inflows. Include grants, loans, investments, and other expected receipts, clearly distinguishing confirmed funding from uncertain possibilities.
  5. List recurring expenses. Include payroll, software, rent, professional services, and other operating payments.
  6. Estimate variable expenses. Calculate the costs that change with sales or delivery volume.
  7. Add planned investments. Use your Ops & HR plan to include hiring costs, equipment purchases, and other growth-related expenses in the appropriate months.
  8. Calculate monthly cash balances. Determine total inflows, total outflows, net cash flow, and closing cash for each month.
  9. Identify your lowest cash position. Look for months when cash may become insufficient to support operations.
  10. Build alternative scenarios. Compare your base forecast with conservative and growth scenarios.
  11. Identify potential funding needs. Determine whether additional capital may be required, how much, and when.
  12. Set a review schedule. Update the forecast monthly using actual results and revised assumptions.

Before moving forward, ask yourself:

  • Do I understand the difference between sales, profit, and cash flow?
  • Have I based my forecast on the sales and operating plans I've developed?
  • Have I considered when customers will actually pay?
  • Have I included payroll, taxes, software, suppliers, and other recurring obligations?
  • Have I included the one-time investments needed for growth?
  • Have I accounted for costs that increase as sales grow?
  • Have I clearly identified assumptions and uncertain funding?
  • Do I know when my cash balance is expected to be lowest?
  • What happens if sales are delayed or expenses increase?
  • Can I afford my planned hiring and investments?
  • Do I know when I may need additional capital?
  • Have I established a process for updating my forecast?

Consider reviewing your forecast with your TechAlliance advisor and, where appropriate, an accountant or financial professional.

docs.title: Prepare for funding analysis
docs.text:
Your cash flow forecast should help you identify:

  • How much funding may be needed: The projected shortfall plus an appropriate operating buffer.
  • When funding may be needed: The period before your cash position becomes insufficient.
  • What the funding would support: Operating expenses, hiring, equipment, inventory, product development, or other business needs.
  • How long the funding could last: The expected runway under different scenarios.
  • What could change the requirement: Sales performance, payment timing, cost reductions, or changes to your growth plan.

Keep these findings available for your upcoming funding analysis.

Remember: A cash flow forecast isn't a prediction you need to get exactly right.

It's a tool for understanding your business, testing your assumptions, and making informed financial decisions.

The more consistently you update it, the more useful it becomes.

docs.title: Choose the right capital to support your business goals
docs.text:
You've researched your market, validated your solution, developed your sales process, planned your operations, and built a cash flow forecast.

Now it's time to bring that information together and decide how your business will finance its next stage.

Funding analysis is the process of evaluating how much capital your company needs, when it needs it, what the money will accomplish, and which financing options best support your goals.

For some businesses, the right approach may be to grow through customer revenue and reinvest profits.

Others may need loans, grants, investors, or a combination of funding sources to develop products, expand operations, or enter new markets.

The right choice depends on your business model, growth ambitions, financial position, risk tolerance, and long-term plans.

Your funding analysis should help you answer:

  • How much money does the business need?
  • What will the money be used for?
  • When will it be needed?
  • How long will it support operations and growth?
  • What milestones should the funding help us achieve?
  • Which funding sources are realistic for our company?
  • What are the costs, risks, and obligations of each option?
  • How will today's financing decisions affect our future opportunities?

The goal isn't to raise as much money as possible. It's to secure the resources your business needs under terms that support its long-term success.

docs.title: Build your funding analysis on everything you've learned
docs.text:
Your funding strategy shouldn't be developed in isolation.

Every stage of your business development journey provides information that can help you determine whether funding is necessary and how it should be used.

docs.title: Idea: Understand the opportunity
docs.text:
Your early research helps explain:

  • The problem you're addressing
  • The potential market
  • Your customer segments
  • The competitive landscape
  • Your initial business model
  • The opportunity you're pursuing

This information helps establish why your business exists and what potential it may have.

docs.title: Discovery: Understand the customer and your approach
docs.text:
Your customer discovery work, expert interviews, product roadmap, and GTM planning help you explain:

  • Which customer problems you've investigated
  • What you've learned from potential customers
  • Which assumptions have been supported or challenged
  • How your proposed solution addresses the problem
  • How you intend to reach customers
  • What remains uncertain

This information can help you explain your strategy and the evidence behind it.

docs.title: Validation: Demonstrate customer value
docs.text:
Your MVP, pilot, solution interviews, and testing results provide evidence about:

  • Whether customers can use your offering
  • Whether it delivers meaningful value
  • How customers respond to pricing
  • What adoption and engagement look like
  • Which improvements are still required
  • What you've learned about commercial potential

Actual customer behaviour is generally stronger evidence than unsupported projections.

Be clear about what has been demonstrated and what still needs testing.

docs.title: Efficiency: Understand what growth will require
docs.text:
Your sales process, Ops & HR plan, and cash flow forecast help you estimate:

  • Expected sales and customer acquisition
  • Current operating capacity
  • Hiring and resource requirements
  • Recurring expenses
  • Planned investments
  • Cash runway
  • Potential funding gaps
  • The financial implications of growth

These plans should form the foundation of your funding requirements.

Your funding analysis connects the opportunity you've identified, the evidence you've gathered, and the business you're preparing to build.

docs.title: Determine whether you need external funding
docs.text:
Before exploring funding sources, consider whether your company actually needs outside capital.

External financing can help you grow, but it also introduces obligations, costs, or changes to ownership.

Ask yourself:

  • Can we finance our next steps through existing cash and customer revenue?
  • Could we reduce or delay some planned expenses?
  • Could customer deposits, advance payments, or recurring revenue improve our cash position?
  • Would slower growth allow us to maintain greater financial independence?
  • Are there investments we need to make before we can generate additional revenue?
  • What opportunities might we miss if we don't secure funding?
  • What risks would external financing introduce?

For example, a service business with modest startup costs and paying customers may be able to grow without investors.

A company developing capital-intensive technology may need substantial funding before it can begin generating meaningful revenue.

Neither approach is automatically better.

Funding should support a clear business need or opportunity, not become a goal on its own.

docs.title: Calculate how much funding you need
docs.text:
Start with your cash flow forecast.

Identify the periods when your business may not have enough cash to cover planned expenses and maintain an appropriate operating buffer.

Consider three components.

docs.title: 1. Operating requirements
docs.text:
How much cash will you need to keep the business running?

This may include:

  • Payroll and contractor payments
  • Software and infrastructure
  • Rent and utilities
  • Customer support
  • Materials and supplies
  • Insurance
  • Professional services
  • Other recurring expenses

docs.title: 2. Planned investments
docs.text:
What additional spending is required to achieve your goals?

Examples include:

  • Hiring employees
  • Developing new product capabilities
  • Purchasing equipment
  • Expanding production
  • Entering new markets
  • Building sales and marketing capacity
  • Meeting regulatory or technical requirements

Connect each major investment to a specific business objective.

docs.title: 3. Operating buffer
docs.text:
How much additional cash should you maintain to manage uncertainty?

Your buffer should reflect the risks and cash requirements of your business.

For example, a company with unpredictable sales and long customer payment cycles may need a larger buffer than a business with stable recurring revenue.

Avoid using a universal buffer percentage without considering your circumstances.

docs.title: Estimate your funding requirement
docs.text:
A practical approach is to:

  1. Start with your current cash balance.
  2. Project future cash inflows and outflows.
  3. Identify the lowest projected cash balance.
  4. Determine the minimum cash reserve your business should maintain.
  5. Calculate the additional capital required to avoid falling below that reserve.
  6. Consider financing costs, transaction expenses, and the timing of funding.

For example, imagine your forecast shows that your cash balance will fall to negative $40,000 before customer revenue begins covering expenses.

If you want to maintain a $20,000 operating reserve, your preliminary funding requirement would be $60,000.

You would then need to consider any financing costs, timing differences, and changes to your operating assumptions.

The result should be a reasoned estimate, not simply an amount that sounds attractive to investors or lenders.

docs.title: Connect funding to future milestones
docs.text:
Funders will often want to understand what their money will help your company accomplish.

Even if you're financing the business yourself, this is a useful planning exercise.

Define the milestones you want to reach with the available capital.

Examples include:

  • Completing an essential product development phase
  • Reaching a defined number of paying customers
  • Establishing a repeatable sales process
  • Increasing production capacity
  • Hiring critical team members
  • Reaching a revenue target
  • Improving gross margins
  • Achieving positive operating cash flow

Choose milestones that reflect meaningful business progress.

For each milestone, estimate:

  • What needs to happen
  • The resources required
  • The expected cost
  • The anticipated timeframe
  • How you'll measure completion
  • What happens if the milestone takes longer than expected

Your funding plan should explain how the capital supports these activities.

A strong funding strategy connects money to measurable progress, rather than treating financing as an end in itself.

docs.title: Understand the main funding methods
docs.text:
Startups can access capital in several ways.

Some options require repayment. Others involve giving investors an ownership interest in the company. Some provide funding without either obligation, although eligibility and other conditions may apply.

docs.title: Bootstrapping and customer-funded growth
docs.text:
Bootstrapping means building and growing your business using founder resources, customer revenue, and cash generated by operations rather than relying primarily on external investors.

Potential advantages include:

  • Maintaining ownership and decision-making control
  • Avoiding investor expectations
  • Reducing dependence on future fundraising
  • Encouraging disciplined spending

Potential limitations include:

  • Slower growth
  • Limited resources for major investments
  • Greater pressure on personal or business cash
  • Difficulty financing capital-intensive activities

Customer deposits, advance payments, subscriptions, and reinvested operating cash may help fund growth.

However, make sure your company can fulfil the obligations associated with advance payments.

Bootstrapping can be an intentional long-term strategy, not simply a temporary step before raising investment.

docs.title: Friends and family
docs.text:
Some founders raise initial capital from people in their personal networks.

This may take the form of:

  • A personal gift
  • A loan
  • An equity investment
  • A convertible investment agreement

The terms matter more than the relationship.

A loan must be evaluated differently from an equity investment, and a gift may have different tax or legal implications.

Potential advantages include access to capital from people who already know and trust the founder.

However, financial losses, misunderstandings, or unmet expectations can damage personal relationships.

If you're considering this approach:

  • Explain the risks clearly.
  • Don't promise returns you cannot support.
  • Document the terms.
  • Clarify whether the money is a gift, loan, or investment.
  • Discuss repayment or ownership expectations.
  • Ensure everyone understands that the business may fail.
  • Obtain appropriate legal and tax advice.

Friends-and-family funding isn't available to every founder, and it isn't a prerequisite for building a successful business.

docs.title: Grants and non-repayable contributions
docs.text:
Grants and other contribution programs may provide funding for eligible activities without requiring founders to give up ownership.

Depending on the program, funding may support:

  • Research and development
  • Product innovation
  • Hiring and training
  • Export development
  • Equipment
  • Commercialization
  • Other defined business activities

However, not all government or institutional funding is non-repayable.

Some programs provide repayable contributions or impose other financial obligations.

Grants may also involve:

  • Eligibility restrictions
  • Application deadlines
  • Matching-funding requirements
  • Eligible expense rules
  • Reporting obligations
  • Reimbursement after expenses are incurred
  • Project milestones

A grant award doesn't necessarily mean the money is immediately available.

Review payment timing carefully and reflect it in your cash flow forecast.

Avoid building a business plan that depends entirely on funding you haven't secured.

docs.title: Debt financing
docs.text:
Debt financing involves borrowing money that must generally be repaid according to agreed terms.

Examples include:

  • Business loans
  • Lines of credit
  • Equipment financing
  • Working capital loans
  • Government-backed lending programs
  • Venture debt

Debt may be appropriate when your company has a reasonably predictable ability to make repayments.

Potential advantages include:

  • Retaining ownership
  • Defined repayment terms
  • Access to capital without selling shares
  • Financing assets or working capital needs

Potential limitations include:

  • Interest and financing costs
  • Required repayments regardless of sales performance
  • Collateral or security requirements
  • Personal guarantees in some circumstances
  • Financial covenants or other restrictions

For example, equipment financing may make sense when a company needs machinery that will support predictable production and revenue.

Borrowing to cover ongoing losses without a credible repayment plan may create significant financial risk.

Evaluate the total borrowing cost, repayment schedule, security requirements, and impact on cash flow before proceeding.

docs.title: Equity financing
docs.text:
Equity financing involves raising capital in exchange for an ownership interest in the company.

Investors may include:

  • Angel investors
  • Venture capital firms
  • Strategic or corporate investors
  • Other private investors
  • Investors participating through eligible equity crowdfunding platforms

Unlike conventional debt, equity financing generally doesn't require scheduled principal and interest payments.

However, founders give up part of the company's ownership and may accept additional governance or investor rights.

Potential advantages include:

  • Access to capital without conventional loan repayments
  • Ability to finance higher-risk growth initiatives
  • Potential access to investor expertise and networks
  • Support for longer-term growth strategies

Potential limitations include:

  • Ownership dilution
  • Changes to governance and decision-making
  • Investor reporting requirements
  • Expectations for growth and future returns
  • Legal and transaction costs

Not every company is a good fit for venture capital.

VC investors generally seek businesses with the potential for substantial growth and investment returns.

A profitable company that intends to grow steadily may be better suited to another financing approach.

docs.title: Crowdfunding
docs.text:
Crowdfunding allows a business to raise money from multiple contributors or investors, often through an online platform.

Common models include:

Rewards-based crowdfunding

Supporters contribute money in exchange for a product, reward, or other benefit.

Equity crowdfunding

Eligible investors provide capital in exchange for securities or an ownership interest, subject to applicable securities regulations.

Donation-based crowdfunding

Contributors provide money without expecting a financial return or commercial reward.

Crowdfunding may help businesses test demand, finance development, or build awareness.

However, it can involve platform fees, campaign expenses, fulfilment obligations, regulatory requirements, and reputational risks.

A successful rewards campaign also creates a responsibility to deliver what was promised.

docs.title: Other funding approaches
docs.text:
Depending on your business model and stage, additional options may include:

  • Strategic partnerships: Commercial arrangements in which another organization contributes capital, resources, distribution, or other support.
  • Revenue-based financing: Capital provided in exchange for payments tied to future revenue, subject to the agreement's terms.
  • Invoice financing: Financing secured against or generated from outstanding customer invoices.
  • Purchase-order financing: Funding tied to fulfilling eligible customer orders.
  • Accelerators and incubators: Programs that may provide funding, mentorship, services, or other support, sometimes in exchange for equity.

Each arrangement has its own eligibility requirements, costs, obligations, and risks.

Evaluate the specific terms rather than assuming an entire category works the same way.

docs.title: Understand common investment instruments
docs.text:
A funding source describes where the money comes from.

An investment instrument describes how the financing arrangement is structured.

For example, an angel investor may invest through a direct equity purchase, a SAFE, or a convertible note.

Understanding the difference is important.

docs.title: Priced equity investment
docs.text:
In a priced equity round, investors purchase shares based on a negotiated company valuation.

Two important concepts are:

Pre-money valuation: The agreed value of the company before the new investment.

Post-money valuation: The value immediately after the investment, generally calculated as the pre-money valuation plus the new capital invested.

For example:

A company raises $250,000 at a $1 million pre-money valuation.

Its post-money valuation would be $1.25 million.

The new investor would generally own 20% immediately after the financing, assuming a straightforward share issuance without other adjustments.

In practice, existing options, convertible instruments, and negotiated terms may affect the final ownership calculation.

Priced rounds may also involve different classes of shares and investor rights.

docs.title: Simple Agreement for Future Equity (SAFE)
docs.text:
A SAFE is an agreement in which an investor provides capital today in exchange for the right to receive equity if specified future events occur.

SAFEs are commonly used in early-stage startup financing.

Unlike a conventional loan, a typical SAFE doesn't accrue interest or have a maturity date.

The company generally doesn't issue shares to the investor immediately.

Instead, the agreement defines how the investment may convert into equity later.

Common terms include:

Valuation cap

A contractual valuation threshold used when calculating the investor's conversion price.

Discount

A provision that may allow the investor to convert at a lower price than investors in a future financing round.

Pre-money or post-money structure

Different approaches to calculating how the SAFE affects ownership and dilution.

Conversion events

Events, such as certain future financing transactions, that may trigger conversion.

SAFEs can simplify early fundraising, but they aren't risk-free or automatically founder-friendly.

Issuing multiple SAFEs can create significant future dilution.

Different SAFE versions and terms can also produce different ownership outcomes.

Before signing a SAFE, model how it could affect your ownership under several future financing scenarios.

Have a qualified lawyer review the agreement, including its suitability for your jurisdiction.

docs.title: Convertible notes
docs.text:
A convertible note is a debt instrument that may convert into company equity when specified conditions are met.

Unlike a typical SAFE, convertible notes generally include:

  • A principal loan amount
  • An interest rate
  • A maturity date
  • Conversion provisions
  • Potential valuation caps or discounts

For example, an investor might lend money to a startup with the expectation that the loan will convert into shares during a future equity financing.

If the relevant conversion event doesn't occur, the agreement may require repayment, renegotiation, or another outcome.

The specific terms determine what happens.

Convertible notes can provide flexibility, but founders should understand both the debt obligations and potential future dilution.

docs.title: Venture debt
docs.text:
Venture debt is a specialized form of lending generally intended for certain venture-backed companies.

It may be used to extend runway or finance growth without immediately raising another equity round.

Unlike conventional business lending, venture debt may include warrants that give the lender the right to acquire shares under specified conditions.

It also involves repayment obligations and may include financial covenants.

Venture debt isn't a general substitute for equity funding and may not be available or suitable for companies without institutional investment backing.

docs.title: Compare funding options before choosing
docs.text:
Each financing method has different implications.

Funding method Repayment obligation Potential ownership dilution Main consideration Bootstrapping No external financing repayment No Growth limited by available resources Customer-funded growth Customer delivery obligations No Must fulfil customer commitments Friends and family Depends on arrangement Depends on arrangement Financial and personal relationship risks Grants Depends on program Usually no Eligibility, restrictions, and payment timing Conventional debt Yes Usually no Repayment capacity and borrowing terms Priced equity No scheduled loan repayment Yes Ownership, control, and investor expectations SAFE Typically no loan repayment Potential future dilution Conversion terms and future ownership Convertible note Debt terms apply Potential future dilution Interest, maturity, and conversion terms Rewards crowdfunding Fulfilment obligations No Campaign costs and delivery commitments Equity crowdfunding No scheduled loan repayment Yes Securities compliance and investor management

This is a simplified comparison.

Actual obligations depend on the agreements, program requirements, and applicable laws.

When comparing options, consider:

  • Total cost of capital
  • Impact on cash flow
  • Ownership dilution
  • Decision-making control
  • Security or personal guarantees
  • Investor or lender expectations
  • Eligibility and availability
  • Time required to secure funding
  • Reporting and compliance obligations
  • Flexibility for future financing

The cheapest-looking option isn't always the most suitable.

For example, a low-interest loan may be inappropriate if your business cannot reliably make the repayments.

Similarly, an equity investment may provide more financial flexibility today but involve substantial long-term ownership costs.

docs.title: Understand dilution and future ownership
docs.text:
If you're considering equity financing, SAFEs, or convertible notes, you need to understand how future transactions may affect ownership.

Dilution occurs when additional shares are issued and existing shareholders own a smaller percentage of the company.

For example, if you currently own 100% of your company and issue shares representing 20% of the company after a financing round, your ownership would generally fall to 80%, assuming no other changes.

Future financing rounds, employee stock options, and convertible instruments may cause additional dilution.

However, a smaller percentage of a more valuable company may still represent a positive outcome.

The important question is whether the financing creates enough value to justify the ownership and other rights being exchanged.

Before accepting investment:

  • Review your current ownership structure.
  • Understand any existing convertible agreements.
  • Model the proposed financing.
  • Consider potential future rounds.
  • Review investor rights and governance terms.
  • Understand how employee equity plans may affect ownership.

Maintain an accurate capitalization table (cap table) showing who owns shares and other relevant equity interests.

Don't evaluate an investment offer based only on the amount of money being provided.

docs.title: Consider how funding decisions affect future growth
docs.text:
Financing decisions can influence your business long after the money has been spent.

For example:

A large equity round may allow you to hire quickly, but it may also create expectations for rapid growth and future fundraising.

A loan may preserve ownership, but its repayments could limit your ability to invest in product development.

A grant may reduce your funding requirements, but eligible expenses or reimbursement schedules could constrain how and when the money is used.

A SAFE may provide capital without immediate debt repayments, but future conversion could affect your ownership more than expected.

Consider how each option fits your intended business trajectory.

Ask yourself:

  • What kind of company are we trying to build?
  • How quickly do we want or need to grow?
  • What risks are we prepared to accept?
  • How much ownership and control do we want to retain?
  • Will this financing create obligations that affect future decisions?
  • Could this arrangement make future financing more difficult?
  • What happens if we don't reach our planned milestones?
  • What would a successful outcome look like for both the founders and funders?

A good funding decision supports the business you want to build, not just the expenses you need to pay today.

docs.title: Prepare for funding conversations
docs.text:
If you decide to pursue external financing, organize the information potential lenders, investors, or funding programs may request.

The requirements will vary.

For example, a lender may focus on repayment capacity, financial history, security, and cash flow.

An equity investor may place greater emphasis on market opportunity, customer traction, growth potential, team capabilities, and future returns.

Your preparation may include:

  • Business overview and value proposition
  • Market and competition analysis
  • Customer segment research
  • Product or service description
  • Customer validation evidence
  • Sales and GTM strategy
  • Current traction and performance
  • Operations and hiring plan
  • Cash flow forecast
  • Funding requirement and intended use
  • Growth milestones
  • Financial statements, where available
  • Ownership and capitalization information
  • Relevant legal and corporate records

Use the information you've already developed rather than creating disconnected versions of your business plan for every conversation.

Keep your assumptions, figures, and claims consistent.

If you haven't yet established an organized company data room, this is a good time to review your document management practices.

Share sensitive information selectively and use appropriate access controls.

docs.title: Funding requirements worksheet
docs.text:
Use your cash flow forecast to estimate the amount and timing of funding your business may need.

Planning element Your estimate Current available cash Forecast period Lowest projected cash balance before new funding Minimum operating reserve Preliminary funding requirement Expected financing and transaction costs Total proposed funding amount Date funding needs to be available Main purpose of the funding Milestones the funding should support

Use your conservative, base, and growth scenarios to test whether the proposed amount is appropriate.

docs.title: Use-of-funds plan
docs.text:
Describe how you intend to allocate the money you raise.

Use of funds Amount Timing Expected business outcome Product development Hiring Sales and marketing Equipment and infrastructure Working capital Other

Use categories relevant to your business.

Ensure that the total aligns with your funding requirement and cash flow forecast.

docs.title: Funding options comparison matrix
docs.text:
Compare realistic funding methods using consistent criteria.

Criteria Option A Option B Option C Funding source Amount potentially available Eligibility Repayment requirements Potential dilution Cost of capital Restrictions or obligations Expected timing Main risks Fit with business goals

Avoid comparing options that aren't realistically available to your business.

docs.title: Milestone-based funding plan
docs.text:
Connect the financing requirement to the outcomes it should support.

Milestone Required activities Estimated cost Target date Success measure

Use realistic milestones based on your operating capacity, sales assumptions, and customer evidence.

docs.title: Ownership and dilution scenario
docs.text:
If you're considering equity or convertible financing, model the potential impact on ownership.

Start by recording:

  • Current shareholders and ownership percentages
  • Existing options or convertible instruments
  • Proposed investment amount
  • Proposed valuation or conversion terms
  • Any planned employee equity pool
  • Potential future financing scenarios

Compare the ownership structure before and after each scenario.

For SAFEs and convertible notes, use a model that reflects the specific agreement terms.

A simple percentage calculation may not capture the effects of valuation caps, discounts, option pools, or multiple convertible instruments.

Have a qualified professional review important assumptions before making financing commitments.

docs.title: Funding readiness checklist
docs.text:

  • [ ] Ownership and capitalization information
  • [ ] Organized company documentation
  • [ ] Understanding of financing risks and obligations

The exact requirements will depend on the type of funding you're pursuing.
