docs.title: Put it into practice
docs.text:
Develop a funding strategy that supports your company's next stage of growth.

By the end of this exercise, you should understand whether you need external funding, how much you may need, what it should accomplish, and which financing approaches are worth exploring.

Start by reviewing your work from the Idea, Discovery, Validation, and Efficiency stages.

Then:

  1. Review your business goals. Define what you want the company to accomplish over the next 12 to 24 months.
  2. Review your cash flow forecast. Identify projected cash shortages, major investments, and the timing of potential funding needs.
  3. Challenge the need for external funding. Consider whether customer revenue, expense adjustments, or slower growth could support your objectives.
  4. Calculate your funding requirement. Estimate the capital needed to cover planned activities and maintain an appropriate operating buffer.
  5. Define the use of funds. Explain how the money will be allocated and what each major expense is intended to achieve.
  6. Identify business milestones. Connect the funding to measurable progress in product development, sales, operations, or financial performance.
  7. Research funding options. Explore bootstrapping, grants, loans, equity investment, SAFEs, convertible notes, and other relevant approaches.
  8. Compare the trade-offs. Evaluate repayment obligations, ownership dilution, financing costs, restrictions, timing, and fit with your goals.
  9. Model different scenarios. Consider what happens if funding is delayed, the amount raised is lower than expected, or business performance differs from your forecast.
  10. Prepare supporting information. Organize your business plans, customer evidence, financial projections, ownership records, and other relevant documents.
  11. Identify your preferred approach. Select the funding options that best match your business needs and circumstances.
  12. Define your next steps. Establish a timeline for researching programs, meeting potential funders, preparing applications, or seeking professional advice.

Before moving forward, ask yourself:

  • Do we actually need external funding to achieve our goals?
  • How much capital do we need, and when?
  • What evidence supports our funding requirement?
  • What specific milestones will the funding help us reach?
  • Can our company support the repayment obligations of debt?
  • Are we comfortable with the ownership dilution associated with equity financing?
  • Do we understand the implications of SAFEs and convertible notes?
  • Are there grants or other funding programs relevant to our activities?
  • Have we considered how funding decisions may affect future financing?
  • What happens if the expected funding doesn't arrive?
  • Does our strategy support the kind of company we want to build?
  • Have we identified where legal, accounting, or financial advice is needed?

Consider discussing your analysis with your TechAlliance advisor before committing to a financing strategy.

For significant debt, equity, SAFE, or convertible note transactions, seek advice from qualified legal and financial professionals.

docs.title: Prepare your funding analysis summary
docs.text:
Bring your findings together in a short document that includes:

1. Business objectives

What the company intends to accomplish over the next planning period.

2. Financial position

Current cash, forecast expenses, expected revenue, and projected runway.

3. Funding requirement

How much capital is needed and when it must be available.

4. Use of funds

How the capital will support operations, investments, and growth.

5. Funding options

The approaches considered and their main advantages, limitations, and risks.

6. Preferred financing strategy

The option or combination of options that appears most appropriate and why.

7. Milestones and expected outcomes

What the company intends to achieve with the funding.

8. Risks and alternative scenarios

What could change the plan and how the business might respond.

9. Next steps

The research, applications, conversations, and professional advice required before proceeding.

Remember: Funding is a means to build a stronger business, not a measure of success on its own.

The right financing strategy should reflect what you've learned about your customers, the value of your solution, your ability to generate revenue, and the resources needed to operate and grow.

Your goal is to make decisions that give your company the financial capacity, flexibility, and time it needs to thrive.

docs.title: Build the capacity to deliver today and grow tomorrow
docs.text:
You've tested your solution, started developing your sales process, and identified how you want to reach more customers.

Now you need to make sure your business can deliver what it sells.

An operations and human resources (Ops & HR) plan describes how your company will organize its people, processes, tools, and other resources to deliver its products or services.

It also identifies what will need to change as your business grows.

At this stage, you don't need a complex organizational structure or a detailed operations manual covering every activity.

You need a practical plan that answers two questions:

  1. Can we reliably deliver our current offering at the service level we've promised?
  2. What additional people, resources, and investments will we need as demand increases?

Your plan should help you:

  • Understand how your business delivers value to customers
  • Define responsibilities and essential workflows
  • Estimate how many customers you can currently serve
  • Identify operational bottlenecks and risks
  • Establish basic people management practices
  • Plan future hiring, equipment, software, and infrastructure needs
  • Estimate the costs and timing of growth
  • Prepare reliable assumptions for cash flow forecasting and funding analysis

The goal isn't to build a large organization before you need one. It's to understand what your business needs today and what it will take to support the next stage of growth.

docs.title: Define the service level you want to deliver
docs.text:
Start by defining what customers should consistently expect from your business.

Your service level describes the quality, availability, responsiveness, and reliability of the product or service you intend to provide.

For example, depending on your offering, customers may expect:

  • Delivery within a specific timeframe
  • Responses to support requests within one business day
  • Reliable access to a software platform
  • A consistent onboarding experience
  • Regular progress updates
  • Products that meet defined quality requirements
  • Access to a particular level of expertise

You don't need to promise the fastest response or highest level of service in your industry.

You need to establish expectations that matter to customers and that your business can realistically meet.

Review your customer discovery findings, solution interviews, pilot results, and sales commitments.

Ask yourself:

  • What do customers need from us to receive the intended value?
  • What have we promised during sales conversations?
  • What level of service can we currently deliver?
  • Which activities are essential to maintaining quality?
  • What would happen if customer demand increased?

Be specific where possible.

For example, "provide excellent customer support" is difficult to plan around.

"Respond to customer support requests within one business day" gives you a clearer operational requirement.

Avoid making commitments that your current resources cannot support.

docs.title: Map how your business delivers value
docs.text:
Once you've defined your service level, identify the activities required to deliver it.

Think about what happens after a customer agrees to purchase your offering.

Depending on your business, the process might include:

  1. Receiving and confirming the order or agreement
  2. Collecting customer requirements
  3. Preparing or configuring the product or service
  4. Delivering the offering
  5. Providing onboarding or training
  6. Responding to customer questions
  7. Monitoring quality and resolving problems
  8. Managing ongoing service or renewals

For a software company, the process may involve account setup, hosting, product maintenance, security, and customer support.

For a consulting business, it may involve project scoping, assigning team members, delivering services, and reviewing results.

For a physical product business, it may involve purchasing materials, manufacturing, inventory, quality control, and shipping.

Map the activities that matter most to your business.

For each activity, identify:

  • Who is responsible
  • What resources are required
  • How much time it takes
  • What tools or systems are involved
  • What could delay or interrupt delivery
  • How you'll know the activity was completed successfully

You don't need to document every minor task.

Focus on the workflows that directly affect your ability to serve customers.

docs.title: Understand your current operating capacity
docs.text:
Before planning growth, establish how much your business can deliver with its current resources.

Operating capacity is the amount of work your business can complete within a given period while maintaining its intended service level.

Your capacity may depend on:

  • Available working hours
  • Employee or founder expertise
  • Equipment and production capabilities
  • Software or infrastructure limits
  • Supplier availability
  • Physical space
  • Customer support requirements
  • Time spent on administration and management

For example, a consulting startup might estimate that each client requires 20 hours of delivery work per month.

If the team has 100 hours available for client delivery, its theoretical capacity would be five clients.

However, the team may need to reserve time for unexpected issues, internal meetings, training, and other responsibilities.

Your practical capacity may therefore be lower.

Similarly, a manufacturing business might have equipment capable of producing 500 units per month but only enough labour or materials to deliver 300.

The lowest relevant constraint determines its current capacity.

docs.title: Identify your bottlenecks
docs.text:
A bottleneck is an activity or resource that limits how much work your business can complete.

Common examples include:

  • One founder approving every customer deliverable
  • Limited manufacturing equipment
  • A shortage of qualified technical staff
  • Manual onboarding that takes too much time
  • Dependence on one supplier
  • Customer support handled by someone who also manages sales

Identifying bottlenecks helps you decide where additional resources or process improvements would make the biggest difference.

Don't assume hiring is always the answer.

Sometimes a clearer process, better software, improved scheduling, or a reliable external provider can increase capacity without adding a permanent employee.

docs.title: Define roles and responsibilities
docs.text:
Even a small startup benefits from clear responsibilities.

Start by listing the functions required to operate your business.

These might include:

  • Leadership and business planning
  • Product development
  • Service delivery or production
  • Sales and marketing
  • Customer onboarding and support
  • Finance and administration
  • People management
  • Technology and information security
  • Legal and compliance coordination

You don't need a separate employee for every function.

In an early-stage startup, one founder may handle several responsibilities.

The important thing is to identify who is accountable for each activity.

For example:

Function Current owner Additional support needed? Product development Founder A Sales Founder B Customer onboarding Founder A Customer support Founder A Bookkeeping External provider HR administration Founder B

Look for responsibilities that are unclear, duplicated, or concentrated in one person.

Consider what would happen if that person became unavailable.

A simple organizational chart or responsibility table is often enough at this stage.

docs.title: Establish essential people management practices
docs.text:
Human resources planning isn't only about deciding when to hire.

It's also about creating an environment where people understand their responsibilities, have the tools to perform their work, and receive appropriate support.

If you already have employees, consider whether you've established basic practices for:

  • Employment agreements and role expectations
  • Compensation and payroll
  • Working hours, time off, and applicable employment standards
  • Workplace health and safety
  • Employee onboarding
  • Training and professional development
  • Performance feedback
  • Communication and collaboration
  • Confidentiality and information security
  • Employee records and privacy

The requirements will depend on your location, industry, workforce, and employment arrangements.

In Ontario, for example, relevant employment standards and workplace obligations may apply even to small businesses.

Consult appropriate government resources or qualified professionals when establishing employment policies, compensation arrangements, or contracts.

docs.title: Prepare for your first hires
docs.text:
If you're not employing anyone yet, you don't need to create a full HR department.

However, you should understand what will be required before hiring your first employee.

Consider:

  • What role is needed?
  • What responsibilities will the person have?
  • What skills and experience are essential?
  • Who will supervise and support them?
  • What compensation can the business afford?
  • What payroll, insurance, and employment obligations apply?
  • What equipment, software, and training will they need?
  • How long will it take them to become productive?

Remember that an employee's cost is more than their salary.

Your financial plan may need to account for employer payroll contributions, benefits, recruiting, equipment, software, training, and other employment-related expenses.

docs.title: Identify the resources required to operate
docs.text:
People are only one part of your operating capacity.

Review the other resources your business needs to deliver its offering.

docs.title: Software and technology
docs.text:
Identify the systems required for product delivery, collaboration, customer management, security, and administration.

For each system, consider:

  • What is it used for?
  • How much does it cost?
  • Is the cost fixed or usage-based?
  • Will the cost increase with more customers or employees?
  • Are there limits that could affect growth?

docs.title: Equipment and infrastructure
docs.text:
Consider computers, production equipment, tools, vehicles, workspace, and other physical resources.

Determine what you already have, what needs maintenance or replacement, and what additional equipment may be required.

docs.title: Suppliers and external providers
docs.text:
Identify external organizations your business depends on.

These might include manufacturers, distributors, cloud providers, contractors, accountants, or specialized service providers.

Consider their capacity, pricing, lead times, reliability, and the consequences of interruptions.

docs.title: Operating expenses
docs.text:
Document the recurring costs required to keep the business running.

Examples include:

  • Salaries and employer-related costs
  • Contractor fees
  • Software subscriptions
  • Rent and utilities
  • Hosting and infrastructure
  • Insurance
  • Equipment maintenance
  • Professional services
  • Materials and supplies
  • Shipping and logistics

Distinguish between costs that remain relatively stable and costs that increase as your business serves more customers.

This distinction will be important for your cash flow forecast.

docs.title: Build a growth plan based on capacity
docs.text:
Once you understand your current operations, plan what needs to change as demand increases.

Avoid assuming that your business will grow at a constant rate or that every additional customer requires the same resources.

Some businesses can serve many more customers with relatively small increases in cost.

Others need additional staff, equipment, or infrastructure at specific points.

For example, a software business may be able to support more users without immediately hiring additional employees, but eventually need more customer support or infrastructure.

A service business may need additional delivery staff much sooner because its capacity depends directly on available working hours.

docs.title: Define growth scenarios
docs.text:
Consider at least three operating scenarios:

Current operations

What does the business need to deliver its existing commitments?

Near-term growth

What would you need if sales increase over the next several months?

Higher-growth scenario

What additional investments would be necessary if demand grows faster than expected?

For each scenario, estimate:

  • Customers or units served
  • Workload and service requirements
  • Staffing needs
  • Equipment and software requirements
  • External provider costs
  • One-time investments
  • Recurring operating expenses
  • Capacity limits and potential bottlenecks

Use your sales goals and pipeline assumptions to inform these scenarios.

Don't assume that your most optimistic sales target will automatically happen.

docs.title: Plan when to hire or invest
docs.text:
A growth plan should explain not only what resources you'll need, but when you'll need them.

For example, you might decide to hire a customer support specialist when the number of active customers reaches a level that the founding team can no longer support reliably.

Or you might need additional production equipment before accepting orders beyond your current manufacturing capacity.

These are capacity triggers: measurable conditions that indicate when a change is needed.

Examples include:

  • Active customer volume
  • Number of projects in progress
  • Production volume
  • Average support response time
  • Staff workload
  • Equipment utilization
  • Delivery backlog
  • Recurring revenue, where it supports the financial commitment

Try to plan ahead of the point where capacity becomes a problem.

Hiring, purchasing equipment, and implementing new systems take time.

For example, if recruiting and onboarding a new employee takes two months, waiting until your team is already overwhelmed may affect customer service.

Include realistic preparation and implementation time in your growth plan.

docs.title: Connect your Ops & HR plan to financial planning
docs.text:
Your operations plan should become a practical input for the cash flow and funding analysis you'll complete later.

The goal is to translate your operating decisions into financial assumptions.

For each planned resource, identify:

  • What: The employee, equipment, software, service, or other resource required
  • Why: The operational need it addresses
  • When: The expected start or purchase date
  • Cost: The estimated one-time and recurring expenses
  • Trigger: The customer demand or operational condition that makes it necessary
  • Lead time: How long it takes to recruit, purchase, implement, or prepare
  • Confidence: Whether the estimate is confirmed, researched, or preliminary

For example:

Resource Trigger Timing One-time cost Recurring cost Customer support employee Customer volume exceeds team capacity Month 7 Recruiting and equipment Salary and employer costs Additional software licences Team grows to five people Month 5 Setup, if applicable Monthly subscriptions Production equipment Forecast orders exceed current capacity Month 10 Equipment purchase Maintenance and operating costs

These are illustrative scenarios, not recommended hiring thresholds.

Your actual plan should use assumptions relevant to your business.

docs.title: Consider the timing of cash outflows
docs.text:
Some investments need to happen before the additional revenue arrives.

For example, you may need to:

  • Hire and train employees before they can serve customers
  • Purchase inventory before receiving customer payments
  • Buy equipment before increasing production
  • Pay software or infrastructure costs before launching a service
  • Cover operating expenses while waiting for customers to pay invoices

This timing matters.

A business can have promising sales opportunities and still face cash flow challenges if it needs to spend money before collecting revenue.

Your Ops & HR plan should help identify these funding requirements before they become urgent.

docs.title: Review and adjust your plan
docs.text:
Your operating plan isn't a fixed commitment to hire or spend according to a predetermined schedule.

It's a working plan that should evolve as your business learns more about demand, delivery costs, and team capacity.

Review it periodically alongside your sales results.

Ask:

  • Are we delivering the service level we promised?
  • Is our team operating at a sustainable workload?
  • Are any bottlenecks becoming more serious?
  • Have our costs changed?
  • Are our growth assumptions still realistic?
  • Do we need to hire, automate, outsource, or change a process?
  • Should any planned investments be delayed or brought forward?

Update the plan when your assumptions change.

Your operations should support your business goals, not create unnecessary costs before the demand exists.

docs.title: Operations and capacity planning worksheet
docs.text:
Use this worksheet to understand how your business currently delivers its offering.

Activity Responsible person Time or resources required Current capacity Bottleneck or risk Customer onboarding Product or service delivery Customer support Quality control Administration

Adjust the activities to match your business.

Use actual delivery experience wherever possible.

If you're relying on estimates, identify them as assumptions and update them as you collect data.

docs.title: RACI matrix
docs.text:
A RACI matrix helps clarify responsibilities for important activities.

RACI stands for:

  • Responsible: The person completing the work
  • Accountable: The person ultimately answerable for the result
  • Consulted: People whose input is needed
  • Informed: People who need updates

You don't need to use RACI for every small task.

It can be particularly useful when multiple founders, employees, or contractors are involved in a process.

docs.title: Simple operating procedure template
docs.text:
Document the most important recurring activities using a short standard operating procedure (SOP).

For each process, include:

Process name: What activity does this document cover?

Purpose: Why does the process matter?

Owner: Who is responsible?

Trigger: When does the process begin?

Steps: What needs to happen, and in what order?

Tools and resources: What is required?

Quality check: How do you know the work was completed correctly?

Exceptions: What should happen when something goes wrong?

Start with processes that affect customer delivery, quality, safety, or business continuity.

Avoid creating documentation that your team won't use.

docs.title: HR and staffing plan
docs.text:
Create a simple overview of your current team and anticipated hiring needs.

Role or function Current coverage Future need Hiring trigger Estimated start date Estimated cost Customer support Product development Operations Administration

Include founder responsibilities, contractors, and external providers where relevant.

Consider whether the need is best addressed through a permanent hire, part-time support, outsourcing, or process improvement.

docs.title: Growth scenario planner
docs.text:
Compare your operating requirements under different levels of demand.

Planning element Current Near-term growth Higher growth Customers or units served Required service level Team size and roles Equipment and infrastructure Software and tools External providers Estimated monthly operating costs One-time investments Main capacity constraint

Use your sales forecasts to inform the scenarios.

Record the assumptions behind each estimate.

This worksheet will become a useful starting point for your cash flow and funding analysis.

docs.title: Hiring and investment trigger tracker
docs.text:
Use this tool to plan resource additions before they become urgent.

Resource needed Capacity trigger Preparation time Expected cost Planned timing Decision status New employee Equipment Software upgrade External service provider

Review the tracker as customer demand and sales forecasts change.

A trigger should prompt a decision, not automatically authorize spending.

Confirm that the business still needs the resource and can support the cost before proceeding.

docs.text:
Google Sheets can help you estimate operating capacity, track staffing needs, compare growth scenarios, and organize cost assumptions.

It is a practical starting point for building an Ops & HR plan that can later be connected to financial forecasts.

docs.title: Microsoft Excel
docs.text: Microsoft Excel can help you build more detailed capacity and resource models, including scenarios that compare staffing, equipment, and operating costs at different levels of demand.

docs.title: Trello
docs.text:
Trello can help you organize recurring operational tasks, assign responsibilities, and track work through simple workflows.

It may be useful for small teams that need more structure without adopting a complex operations system.

docs.title: Notion
docs.text:
Notion can help you maintain an internal operations workspace containing responsibilities, SOPs, onboarding materials, and team documentation.

Start with the information your team needs most rather than building an extensive knowledge base immediately.

docs.text: Miro can help you visualize workflows, map responsibilities, identify bottlenecks, and plan how your organizational structure might change as the business grows.

Put it into practice
docs.text:
Create a practical Ops & HR plan that supports your current customers and prepares your business for growth.

By the end of this exercise, you should know what your business needs to operate today, how much it can currently deliver, and what additional resources and costs may be required as demand increases.

Start by reviewing your sales goals, current customer commitments, and findings from your MVP or pilot.

Then:

  1. Define your service level. Describe what customers should consistently expect from your business.
  2. Map your operations. Identify the essential activities required to deliver your product or service.
  3. Assign responsibilities. Document who currently manages each important activity.
  4. Estimate your capacity. Determine how many customers, projects, or units your existing resources can support.
  5. Identify bottlenecks. Find the activities or resources most likely to limit delivery or affect quality.
  6. Review your people practices. Confirm that essential employment, onboarding, communication, and team support needs are addressed.
  7. Inventory your resources. List the people, software, equipment, infrastructure, and external providers required to operate.
  8. Build growth scenarios. Estimate what your business would need at different levels of customer demand.
  9. Plan future hires and investments. Identify the resources you'll need, the conditions that trigger them, and how long they'll take to put in place.
  10. Estimate costs. Record one-time investments, recurring expenses, expected timing, and the assumptions behind your figures.
  11. Document your plan. Bring the information together in a short, practical document or spreadsheet.
  12. Review it regularly. Update your capacity, staffing, and cost assumptions as sales and operational needs change.

Before moving forward, ask yourself:

  • Can we consistently deliver the service level we've promised?
  • Do we understand the activities required to serve each customer?
  • Is someone responsible for every essential function?
  • How much additional demand can we handle with our current resources?
  • What is our most important operational bottleneck?
  • Are we relying too heavily on one person, supplier, or system?
  • Do we have the basic people management practices our team needs?
  • What would need to change if our customer base doubled?
  • When would we need to hire or invest in additional resources?
  • Have we considered the full cost of employees, equipment, software, and external services?
  • Do we know which expenses are one-time and which are recurring?
  • Have we documented when those expenses are likely to occur?

Consider reviewing your plan with your TechAlliance advisor, particularly if you're preparing to hire, expand operations, or seek funding.

docs.title: Prepare for cash flow and funding analysis
docs.text:
Your final Ops & HR plan should include a resource forecast that can be transferred into your financial planning.

At minimum, prepare:

  • Current operating costs: What you spend today to run the business.
  • Planned hires: Roles, expected start dates, and estimated total employment costs.
  • Planned investments: Equipment, infrastructure, software, and other purchases.
  • Growth-related expenses: Costs that increase as customer demand grows.
  • Timing assumptions: When expenses will occur and how far in advance you need to commit.
  • Capacity assumptions: How many customers or units each operating scenario can support.

Keep your estimates realistic and identify where additional research or quotes are needed.

Remember: The purpose of your Ops & HR plan isn't to predict every future operational decision.

It's to make sure you can deliver what you've promised today, recognize what growth will require tomorrow, and understand the financial implications before making major commitments.

A clear plan will help you build a more reliable cash flow forecast and make better decisions about when, why, and how much funding your business may need.

docs.title: Turn your validated solution into a repeatable sales process
docs.text:
You've tested your solution with potential customers, collected feedback, and started understanding what makes people willing to use or pay for your offering.

Now it's time to build a sales process that helps you reach more of the right customers, communicate your value, and turn opportunities into revenue.

During the Discovery stage, you developed a draft go-to-market (GTM) plan. During Validation, you tested your offering and learned more about customer needs, adoption, and willingness to pay.

The Efficiency stage is where you use that evidence to establish more consistent business operations.

A sales process is a defined series of activities your business follows to identify potential customers, understand their needs, present an appropriate solution, and guide them toward a purchasing decision.

Sales assets are the materials and tools that support those activities, such as your website, product descriptions, sales presentations, proposals, and customer relationship management (CRM) system.

Together, they help you:

  • Explain what you sell and who it's for
  • Reach and qualify potential customers
  • Communicate the value of your offering
  • Manage opportunities and follow-ups
  • Coordinate responsibilities across your team
  • Track sales performance
  • Improve your approach as you learn

Your first sales process doesn't need to be complicated.

It should be clear enough that someone else could understand how your business sells, follow the steps, and identify what needs improvement.

The goal isn't to create more paperwork. It's to make sales more consistent, measurable, and manageable as your business grows.

docs.title: Make sure your business is ready to sell
docs.text:
Before setting ambitious sales targets, consider whether your business can deliver what it sells.

More customers can create new operational challenges, particularly when your team is small.

Start by reviewing your business goals and operating capacity.

Ask yourself:

  • What are our revenue and growth goals?
  • How many customers can we currently serve?
  • What would happen if our sales doubled?
  • Do we have enough time, people, equipment, and resources to deliver?
  • What additional costs would growth create?
  • At what point would we need to hire, purchase equipment, or expand our operations?
  • Can we maintain the quality of our offering as demand increases?

For example, a consulting business might be able to serve five additional clients without hiring anyone.

However, serving 20 additional clients could require new employees, software, or other resources.

A product business might face different constraints, such as manufacturing capacity, inventory, infrastructure, or customer support.

Understanding these limits helps you set realistic sales goals and avoid making commitments your business can't fulfil.

If you haven't already documented your business model, consider completing a Business Model Canvas or Lean Canvas.

These tools can help you connect your sales strategy with the rest of your business.

docs.title: Define your ideal customer profile
docs.text:
You may have identified several potential customer segments during Discovery.

Your Validation-stage findings should now help you understand which customers are most likely to benefit from your solution.

Use that evidence to refine your ideal customer profile (ICP).

An ICP describes the characteristics of customers who are a particularly good fit for your offering.

For B2B businesses, these characteristics might include:

  • Industry
  • Company size
  • Geographic location
  • Business model
  • Operational challenges
  • Existing technology or processes
  • Purchasing capacity
  • Relevant growth stage or business circumstances

For B2C businesses, your customer profile may focus more on behaviours, needs, circumstances, and purchasing patterns.

Avoid defining your ICP so broadly that nearly everyone qualifies.

A focused customer profile helps you prioritize opportunities and tailor your sales approach.

docs.title: Identify who makes purchasing decisions
docs.text:
The person who uses your solution isn't always the person who decides to buy it.

For B2B sales, you may need to engage several stakeholders.

For example:

  • End user: The person who will use your product or service.
  • Decision-maker: The person with authority to approve the purchase.
  • Influencer: Someone who helps evaluate or recommend solutions.
  • Budget owner: The person responsible for the relevant spending.
  • Technical or operational stakeholder: Someone who assesses implementation, compatibility, security, or other requirements.

These roles may overlap, particularly in smaller organizations.

Understanding the purchasing process helps you avoid spending time on opportunities that cannot move forward.

Ask who experiences the problem, who benefits from solving it, who approves spending, and what steps are required before a purchase can happen.

docs.title: Set sales goals that match your capacity
docs.text:
Once you've defined your target customers and operating capacity, establish initial sales goals.

Consider:

  • How much revenue do you want to generate monthly or quarterly?
  • How many customers or contracts would that require?
  • What is your expected average sale value?
  • How long does it typically take to close a sale?
  • How many opportunities would you need to reach your target?
  • Can your business deliver that volume profitably?

For example, if your quarterly revenue target is $30,000 and your average sale is $5,000, you would need six completed sales to reach that target.

The next question is how many qualified opportunities you'll need to generate those six sales.

If you don't have enough sales history to estimate conversion rates, start with assumptions and update them as you collect data.

Don't treat early estimates as established benchmarks.

Your sales targets should reflect both your commercial ambitions and your ability to deliver.

docs.title: Create the sales assets your customers need
docs.text:
Sales assets help potential customers understand your offering and make purchasing decisions.

You don't need to create every possible asset immediately.

Start with the materials that support your actual sales process.

docs.title: Website and landing pages
docs.text:
Your website may be the first place a potential customer learns about your business.

Consider how someone unfamiliar with your company would experience it.

Can they quickly understand:

  • What you offer?
  • Who it's for?
  • What problem it solves?
  • What benefits they can expect?
  • Why they should consider your solution?
  • What they should do next?

Use clear, customer-focused language.

Avoid relying on technical terminology or feature lists without explaining the value.

If you serve different customer segments, you may need dedicated pages that address their specific needs.

Make it easy for visitors to take the next step, such as requesting a demonstration, booking a conversation, or making a purchase.

docs.title: Product and service descriptions
docs.text:
Create a clear description of each product or service you're ready to sell.

Include:

  • The customer problem it addresses
  • The intended customer
  • What the offering includes
  • The main benefits or expected outcomes
  • Important limitations or requirements
  • Pricing or how to request a quote
  • The next step to purchase or learn more

Focus on the value customers receive.

For example, instead of only saying:

"Our software includes automated data integration."

Explain the customer benefit:

"Bring sales information from multiple systems into one report, reducing the manual work involved in preparing weekly updates."

Support claims about savings, performance, or other outcomes with evidence where available.

docs.title: Sales pitch
docs.text:
Your sales pitch should help you explain your offering clearly and confidently.

Unlike an investor pitch, a customer-facing sales pitch should focus on the customer's problem, your solution, and the value of addressing that problem.

Prepare different versions for situations such as:

  • A brief introduction at a networking event
  • An initial outreach message
  • A discovery or qualification call
  • A product demonstration
  • A conversation with a purchasing decision-maker

Use your earlier elevator pitch work as a starting point, but adapt it to the customer's context.

docs.title: Sales presentation
docs.text:
A sales deck can help structure conversations with potential customers, especially for B2B products and services.

A useful presentation might cover:

  1. The customer problem
  2. The impact of leaving that problem unresolved
  3. Your proposed solution
  4. How the product or service works
  5. The benefits and outcomes
  6. What makes your approach different
  7. Relevant evidence from customer testing or actual results
  8. The implementation or purchasing process
  9. The next step

Keep the presentation focused on the audience.

Don't overload it with company history or technical details that aren't relevant to the purchasing decision.

docs.title: Proposals, quotes, and pricing information
docs.text:
If your business requires customized proposals or quotes, prepare a reusable template.

Depending on your offering, it might include:

  • Customer needs and objectives
  • Proposed scope of work
  • Deliverables
  • Timeline
  • Pricing and payment terms
  • Responsibilities
  • Assumptions and exclusions
  • Acceptance or approval process

Make sure your pricing reflects your costs, intended margins, and the value you're delivering.

Review significant legal or contractual terms with an appropriate professional when necessary.

docs.title: Supporting materials
docs.text:
Depending on your business, you may also benefit from:

  • Product demonstration scripts
  • Frequently asked questions
  • Onboarding information
  • Comparison sheets
  • Technical specifications
  • Security or compliance information
  • Case studies or testimonials
  • Follow-up email templates

Only use testimonials, performance claims, and customer examples that are genuine and approved for the intended use.

Prioritize the assets customers need to understand, evaluate, and purchase your offering. Add more materials as your sales process develops.

docs.title: Choose how you'll reach potential customers
docs.text:
Return to your GTM planning draft and consider which channels showed the most promise during Validation.

Your sales channels are the ways potential customers discover your offering or connect with your team.

Examples include:

  • LinkedIn outreach
  • Email outreach
  • Networking events
  • Industry associations
  • Referrals
  • Strategic partnerships
  • In-person visits
  • Website inquiries
  • Search engines
  • Social media
  • Paid advertising

Not every channel will be appropriate for your business.

A specialized B2B technology company may benefit from targeted outreach and industry partnerships.

A consumer product business may rely more heavily on online discovery, retail distribution, or direct purchasing.

Start with a manageable number of channels that match your customers' behaviour and your team's resources.

For each channel, define:

  • Who you're trying to reach
  • Why the channel is appropriate
  • What message or offer you'll use
  • What action you want the prospect to take
  • Who will manage the activity
  • How you'll measure the results

Follow applicable privacy, consent, and anti-spam requirements when conducting outreach.

Your channel strategy determines how potential customers enter your sales funnel.

Your sales process determines what happens next.

docs.title: Define your sales funnel and process
docs.text:
A sales funnel describes how potential customers move from initial awareness toward a purchase.

A sales pipeline tracks individual opportunities as they progress through defined stages.

A sales process describes the actions your team takes to help customers move through those stages.

For example, a B2B sales process might include:

Stage Objective Typical activities Lead generation Identify potential customers Research, outreach, referrals, inbound inquiries Qualification Determine whether there's a potential fit Understand needs, budget, decision-makers, and timing Discovery Understand the customer's situation Ask questions, identify requirements, clarify desired outcomes Presentation or demonstration Show how your solution addresses the need Tailored pitch, product demonstration, relevant materials Proposal or quote Present a commercial offer Scope, pricing, timeline, terms Negotiation and decision Address questions and reach a decision Follow-ups, approvals, contract discussions Closed won or lost Record the outcome Confirm purchase or document why the opportunity didn't proceed Customer handoff Prepare for successful delivery Share commitments, requirements, and onboarding information

Your business may need fewer or different stages.

For example, an online store may have a largely self-service purchasing process.

A complex enterprise solution may involve several demonstrations, technical reviews, and procurement steps.

Design the process around how your customers actually buy.

docs.title: Define what happens at each stage
docs.text:
For every stage, establish:

  • What qualifies an opportunity to enter the stage
  • What actions your team should take
  • What information needs to be collected
  • Which sales assets should be used
  • Who is responsible
  • What must happen before the opportunity moves forward
  • How and when to follow up

This prevents opportunities from getting lost or remaining in the pipeline without a clear next step.

docs.title: Assign sales responsibilities
docs.text:
A process only works when someone is responsible for executing it.

In an early-stage startup, the founder may manage most sales activities.

As the business grows, responsibilities may be shared among co-founders, employees, contractors, or dedicated sales staff.

Consider who will:

  • Identify and research leads
  • Conduct outreach
  • Qualify opportunities
  • Deliver presentations and demonstrations
  • Prepare proposals
  • Negotiate terms
  • Follow up with prospects
  • Update the CRM
  • Manage the customer handoff
  • Review sales performance

Make responsibilities explicit, even if one person handles several tasks.

If you're considering hiring someone to support sales, document your process before expecting them to execute it independently.

docs.title: Set up your CRM
docs.text:
A customer relationship management (CRM) system helps you organize information about prospects, customers, and sales opportunities.

At an early stage, a well-maintained spreadsheet may be sufficient.

As your sales activity grows, dedicated CRM software can make collaboration, follow-ups, and reporting easier.

At minimum, you should be able to track:

  • Company or customer name
  • Contact information
  • Customer segment
  • Lead source
  • Current sales stage
  • Estimated opportunity value
  • Expected decision or closing date
  • Last interaction
  • Next action and due date
  • Person responsible
  • Final outcome and reason, when known

Keep information accurate and up to date.

Limit access to appropriate team members and handle personal information according to applicable privacy requirements.

A CRM is only useful when your team consistently records and uses the information.

docs.title: Document your process in a sales SOP
docs.text:
Once you've defined your sales activities, bring everything together in a standard operating procedure (SOP).

An SOP is a practical document explaining how a recurring business process should be performed.

Your sales SOP should help someone understand how to manage an opportunity from initial contact to a completed sale or other outcome.

Include:

  • Sales goals and target customer profile
  • Lead generation channels
  • Qualification criteria
  • Sales stages and their definitions
  • Responsibilities
  • Outreach and follow-up procedures
  • Required sales assets
  • CRM instructions
  • Proposal and approval procedures
  • Customer handoff steps
  • Performance metrics
  • Review and improvement schedule

Keep it practical.

A short document with clear steps and links to useful templates is often more valuable than a lengthy manual nobody uses.

Review the SOP as your sales process evolves.

docs.title: Measure and improve your sales performance
docs.text:
Once your process is running, begin tracking how opportunities move through your funnel.

Useful metrics include:

Sales activity

  • Number of prospects contacted
  • Number of responses received
  • Number of discovery calls completed
  • Number of demonstrations delivered
  • Number of proposals sent

Conversion

  • Percentage of leads that become qualified opportunities
  • Percentage of qualified opportunities that reach the proposal stage
  • Percentage of proposals that become sales
  • Overall win rate

Revenue and efficiency

  • Revenue generated
  • Average deal value
  • Average sales cycle length
  • Cost of acquiring a customer
  • Revenue or margin relative to sales effort

Customer insights

  • Reasons opportunities are lost
  • Common objections
  • Frequently requested features
  • Differences between customer segments
  • Feedback about pricing or implementation

Don't measure activity alone.

Sending more messages isn't necessarily an improvement if those messages aren't reaching appropriate customers or generating meaningful opportunities.

Review your results regularly.

For example, if many prospects agree to meetings but few request proposals, investigate what happens during those conversations.

You may need to adjust your qualification criteria, presentation, offering, or customer profile.

If many proposals are sent but few are accepted, investigate pricing, timing, decision-making requirements, or how well the proposal addresses customer needs.

Use sales data to identify where your process needs attention, then make focused improvements and measure the results.

docs.title: Business Model Canvas
docs.text:
The Business Model Canvas helps you describe how your company creates, delivers, and captures value.

Use it to review your customer segments, value proposition, channels, revenue streams, cost structure, and key resources before setting sales goals.

docs.title: Canvanizer
docs.text:
Canvanizer provides an online workspace for completing business canvases, including business model and lean canvas formats.

It can help you organize your business assumptions and identify operational considerations that affect your sales strategy.

docs.title: Ideal customer profile worksheet
docs.text:
Use this worksheet to describe the customers you want to prioritize.

Category Your definition Target customer segment Industry or market Company size or customer characteristics Geographic focus Main customer problem Current alternatives Buying triggers Decision-maker Other purchasing stakeholders Budget or purchasing considerations Reasons a customer may not be a good fit

Base your answers on customer research, Validation-stage findings, and actual sales conversations.

Update the profile as you learn which customers are most likely to buy and benefit from your solution.

docs.title: Sales funnel mapping
docs.text:
Map the stages a prospect moves through before becoming a customer.

For each stage, document:

Sales stage Entry criteria Required action Responsible person Exit criteria Lead Qualified opportunity Discovery Presentation or demo Proposal Decision Closed won/lost

Adjust the stages to reflect your business.

The goal is to establish a process your team can consistently follow and measure.

docs.title: Sales assets checklist
docs.text:
Use this checklist to identify which materials you need to prepare.

  • [ ] Website or landing page with a clear value proposition
  • [ ] Product or service descriptions
  • [ ] Customer-facing sales pitch
  • [ ] Sales presentation or deck
  • [ ] Product demonstration or service explanation
  • [ ] Pricing information
  • [ ] Proposal or quote template
  • [ ] Outreach message templates
  • [ ] Follow-up message templates
  • [ ] Frequently asked questions
  • [ ] Customer onboarding or handoff information
  • [ ] CRM or lead-tracking system

Prioritize assets that directly support your current sales process.

docs.title: Sales goals and funnel calculator
docs.text:
Work backward from your revenue target to estimate the number of opportunities you need.

For example:

Input Example Quarterly revenue target $30,000 Average sale value $5,000 Sales required 6 Assumed proposal-to-sale conversion rate 30% Proposals required 20 Assumed qualified-lead-to-proposal conversion rate 50% Qualified leads required 40

These figures are illustrative, not industry benchmarks.

Use your own data when available and clearly identify assumptions when it isn't.

As your sales process generates more information, update the calculator to improve your planning.

docs.title: Sales SOP template
docs.text:
Create one document that explains how your company manages sales.

Use the following structure:

1. Purpose and goals

What is the process intended to achieve?

2. Target customers

Who are you selling to, and how do you recognize a qualified opportunity?

3. Sales channels

Where do leads come from, and how are they contacted?

4. Sales stages

What are the steps from initial contact to purchase?

5. Activities and responsibilities

What must happen at each stage, and who is responsible?

6. Sales assets

Which templates, presentations, scripts, and other materials should be used?

7. CRM procedures

What information must be recorded and updated?

8. Customer handoff

How are commitments and customer requirements transferred to the person or team delivering the offering?

9. Performance measurement

Which metrics will be tracked, and how often will results be reviewed?

10. Continuous improvement

How will the process be updated based on performance and customer feedback?

docs.title: HubSpot CRM
docs.text:
HubSpot CRM can help you organize contacts, manage sales opportunities, track interactions, and monitor pipeline activity.

It may be a useful starting point for startups moving beyond spreadsheet-based sales tracking.

docs.title: Pipedrive
docs.text:
Pipedrive is a sales-focused CRM that helps teams visualize opportunities, manage activities, and track deals through a pipeline.

It may be useful for businesses with a defined sales process involving multiple conversations or follow-ups.

docs.title: Google Sheets
docs.text:
Google Sheets can help you build an initial sales tracker, map your funnel, estimate sales targets, and monitor conversion rates.

A spreadsheet can be sufficient when your sales volume is low and your process is still evolving.

docs.title: Canva
docs.text:
Canva can help you create sales presentations, product sheets, proposals, and other customer-facing materials.

Use a consistent visual style and focus on clear communication rather than adding unnecessary design elements.

docs.title: Calendly
docs.text:
Calendly can help potential customers book sales conversations or product demonstrations.

It may reduce scheduling effort and make it easier for interested prospects to take the next step.

docs.title: Dock - Startup sales: A guide for founders and first sales hires
Zendesk - Beginner's guide to the sales process for startups
BDC - 6 steps to improving your sales process
Put it into practice
docs.text:
Build the first version of your company's sales process and prepare the assets needed to execute it.

By the end of this exercise, you should have a documented sales process, a clear set of supporting materials, and a way to track opportunities and measure results.

Start by reviewing your GTM planning draft, MVP/Pilot findings, and customer feedback.

Then:

  1. Review your business goals and capacity. Determine how much you want to sell and what your team can realistically deliver.
  2. Refine your ideal customer profile. Identify the customers most likely to benefit from your solution and the people involved in purchasing decisions.
  3. Set initial sales targets. Define revenue or customer acquisition goals for a realistic period.
  4. Review your offering. Make sure you can clearly explain what you're selling, what it includes, and why it matters to customers.
  5. Prepare essential sales assets. Update your website, product descriptions, sales pitch, presentation, and proposal templates as needed.
  6. Choose your sales channels. Identify how you'll reach potential customers and generate opportunities.
  7. Map your sales funnel. Define the stages a prospect moves through before becoming a customer.
  8. Assign responsibilities. Decide who will manage each activity and follow-up.
  9. Set up your CRM. Create a consistent way to record prospects, opportunities, interactions, and next steps.
  10. Document your SOP. Bring your sales process into one practical document that your team can follow.
  11. Start executing. Use the process with real prospects and record what happens.
  12. Review and improve. Track conversion rates, sales activity, revenue, and customer feedback. Update your process as you learn.

Before considering your process ready, ask yourself:

  • Can a potential customer quickly understand what we sell and why it matters?
  • Do we know which customers to prioritize?
  • Have we identified the people involved in purchasing decisions?
  • Are our sales goals realistic given our operating capacity?
  • Do we have the materials needed to support sales conversations?
  • Does every opportunity have a clear next step?
  • Does someone own each stage of the process?
  • Are we consistently recording information in our CRM?
  • Could another team member follow our documented sales process?
  • Do we know which metrics will help us identify problems and opportunities?
  • Have we established a schedule for reviewing and improving the process?

Consider reviewing your sales SOP and supporting materials with your TechAlliance advisor before expanding your outreach efforts or hiring sales staff.

Remember: Your first sales process doesn't need to be perfect.

Start with a clear approach, execute it consistently, measure what happens, and improve it based on evidence.

The goal is to build a sales system that your business can manage, repeat, and eventually grow.

docs.title: Explore your idea and understand its potential
docs.text:
Have an idea for a new business, product, or service? Before investing significant time and resources, it's worth exploring the problem you want to solve, who experiences it, and why your proposed solution might matter.

The Idea stage helps you take a closer look at your opportunity, challenge assumptions, and build a clearer understanding of what you're working toward.

You don't need to have all the answers yet. This is your opportunity to research, ask questions, and explore what's possible.

docs.title: What you'll explore
docs.text:
The resources in this section can help you:

  • Define the problem: Understand the challenge your idea aims to address and why it matters.
  • Identify potential customers: Explore who might benefit from your solution and what their needs may be.
  • Research your market: Learn about your industry, existing solutions, and competitors.
  • Clarify your value proposition: Consider what makes your idea relevant to potential customers.
  • Identify your assumptions: Recognize what you know, what you believe, and what you still need to investigate.

docs.title: How to use these resources
docs.text:
Explore the topics available in this section to develop your understanding of the opportunity you're considering.

Each topic may include practical notes, tools, templates, or links to additional reading that can help you explore different aspects of your idea.

If your TechAlliance advisor has recommended specific resources, start there. You can return to other topics as your questions and priorities evolve.

docs.title: Questions to consider
docs.text:
As you explore your idea, think about:

  • What problem am I trying to solve?
  • Who experiences this problem?
  • How are potential customers addressing it today?
  • What makes my proposed solution worth exploring?
  • What do I still need to learn or validate?

Use these questions to guide your research, identify gaps in your understanding, and prepare for conversations with your TechAlliance advisor.

docs.title: Your next step
docs.text:
Start with the topic that addresses your most important question right now.

Use what you learn to refine your thinking, identify assumptions, and prepare to explore your opportunity further in the Discovery stage.

docs.title: Understand your competition and find opportunities in the market
docs.text:
You're building on your business idea right now, but how are your potential customers solving the same problem today?

Understanding your competition is an important part of exploring a business opportunity. It helps you learn what solutions already exist, how companies attract customers, and where your idea might offer something different.

A competition analysis, also called a competitive analysis, is a structured way to research other businesses and alternatives in your market. It involves comparing their products, pricing, positioning, strengths, weaknesses, and customer experiences.

The goal isn't simply to find out who's competing with you. It's to understand the choices your potential customers have and identify where there may be unmet needs or opportunities worth exploring.

You don't need to know everything about every competitor. Start by building a useful picture of the market and focus on the information that can help you make better decisions.

docs.title: Who are your competitors?
docs.text:
Your competition may extend beyond businesses offering products or services similar to yours.

Consider three types of competition:

  • Direct competitors: Businesses offering similar solutions to the same target customers. For example, two software platforms designed to help small businesses manage their finances.
  • Indirect competitors: Businesses offering different solutions that address a similar customer need. For example, a specialized accounting platform competing with a broader business management platform.
  • Substitutes and alternatives: Other ways customers can solve the problem, including spreadsheets, manual processes, internal teams, or existing tools used for a different purpose.

Sometimes, your biggest competitor is the way customers already do things.

A potential customer may recognize the problem you're trying to solve but still prefer their current approach because it's familiar, affordable, or requires less effort to adopt.

Understanding these alternatives can help you identify what your solution would need to offer to encourage customers to change.

docs.title: What should you research?
docs.text:
Once you've identified potential competitors, take a closer look at how they operate and what customers value about their offerings.

Consider researching:

  • Market presence and positioning: Where do competitors operate, who do they serve, and how do they position themselves? What is known about their market share or business size?
  • Products and services: What solutions do they offer? What features, variations, or service levels are available?
  • Pricing and revenue models: How much do they charge? Do they use subscriptions, one-time purchases, usage-based pricing, or other models?
  • Distribution channels: How do customers access their products or services? Do they sell directly, through partners, or through other channels?
  • Marketing and customer acquisition: How do they reach customers? What messages, channels, and promotional approaches do they use?
  • Value propositions and differentiators: Why might customers choose them? What makes their offerings attractive or difficult to compete with?
  • Target customers: Who appears to use their solutions? What industries, business sizes, locations, or customer groups do they serve?
  • Customer experience and reputation: What do customers appreciate or criticize? What problems remain unresolved?

You may not find reliable information for every category.

Private companies, for example, may not disclose their revenue, market share, or detailed customer demographics.

Separate verified information from estimates and assumptions. If reliable data isn't available, record the gap rather than treating an unsupported estimate as fact.

docs.title: Look beyond the features
docs.text:
It's easy to focus on what competing products can do. However, features are only one part of why customers choose a solution.

Customers may also consider:

  • Price and overall cost
  • Ease of use and implementation
  • Customer support
  • Reliability and quality
  • Availability and delivery time
  • Compatibility with existing tools
  • Brand reputation and trust
  • Switching costs and contractual commitments

For example, a competitor may offer more features than your proposed solution but require a complex setup process.

That could represent an opportunity for a simpler alternative, particularly if your target customers value ease of use.

However, an apparent gap doesn't automatically mean customers want a new solution.

Use your competition analysis to identify questions and assumptions you can investigate further during customer discovery.

docs.title: Competitor comparison matrix
docs.text:
A competitor comparison matrix helps you organize information about different companies in a consistent format.

Start by selecting a manageable group of competitors and alternatives. Include direct competitors as well as other solutions your customers might consider.

Create a table comparing the factors most relevant to your market.

Criteria Your idea Competitor A Competitor B Target customers Main problem addressed Products or services Pricing model Key features Distribution channels Main differentiators Customer feedback

Add or remove criteria based on your business.

For your own idea, distinguish between what you're proposing and what you've already tested or demonstrated.

Use the completed matrix to identify patterns, differences, and questions that deserve further investigation.

docs.title: Perceptual map
docs.text:
A perceptual map, also called a positioning map, is a visual tool that helps you compare how different solutions are positioned or perceived in the market.

It typically uses two axes representing characteristics that matter to customers.

For example, you could compare:

  • Price versus perceived quality
  • Ease of use versus available features
  • Level of customization versus implementation complexity
  • Customer support versus cost

Place each competitor on the map according to its position on those two characteristics.

You can also include your proposed solution to visualize where you intend to compete.

A perceptual map can help you identify crowded areas of the market, possible positioning opportunities, and differences between competitors.

Choose characteristics that matter to your target customers. A map based on irrelevant factors may look useful without providing meaningful insight.

Whenever possible, use customer feedback, research, or measurable information to support where you place each competitor.

If you're relying on your own judgement, label the map as an initial estimate that still needs validation.

docs.title: Competitive strengths and weaknesses analysis
docs.text:
Once you've gathered information, review what each competitor appears to do well and where customers may experience difficulties.

Consider:

  • What are their strongest competitive advantages?
  • What do customers consistently value about their solutions?
  • What complaints or limitations appear repeatedly?
  • Which strengths would be difficult for a new business to replicate?
  • Where might there be opportunities to serve customers differently?

Look for patterns across several competitors rather than relying on a single review or observation.

Use your findings to identify potential opportunities, but avoid assuming that every competitor weakness represents an unmet customer need.

docs.title: ChatGPT / Claude / DeepSeek / Augure[1]
docs.text:
"Traditional" LLM tools can help you organize competitor research, identify potential alternatives, compare publicly available information, and summarize your findings.

When web research is available, you can use it to investigate competitor websites, pricing, positioning, and customer feedback.

Use the suggested research prompt below as a starting point, and review the sources behind important claims before relying on the results.

[1]: Augure is the only fully Canadian option from this list

docs.title: Perplexity
docs.text:
Perplexity is an AI-powered research and search tool that can help you explore competitors, find relevant online sources, and investigate market information.

It can be useful for discovering companies you may not have considered and collecting initial information about their products, positioning, and public presence.

Check the original sources, especially when reviewing financial information, market estimates, or claims about competitors.

docs.title: Suggested AI research prompt
docs.text:
You can use the following prompt with an AI research tool that supports web searches.

Replace the information in brackets with details about your business.

Act as an experienced market research analyst specializing in competitive analysis for startups.

I'm exploring a venture called [VENTURE NAME].

Website (if available): [WEBSITE URL]
Proposed products or services: [DESCRIPTION]
Business location: [CITY, PROVINCE/STATE, COUNTRY]
Target markets: [GEOGRAPHIC MARKETS OR ONLINE]
Target customers: [CUSTOMER DESCRIPTION]
Problem we aim to solve: [CUSTOMER PROBLEM]

I need you to research our competitive landscape, including direct competitors, indirect competitors, and alternative ways customers currently solve the same problem.

Use credible, publicly available sources and provide links to support your findings.

PART 1: IDENTIFY THE COMPETITION

Create a table identifying relevant competitors and alternatives.

For each one, include:
- Company or solution name
- Website
- Headquarters or operating location, if known
- Geographic markets served
- Type of competition (direct, indirect, or substitute)
- Brief explanation of why customers might consider this alternative

PART 2: RESEARCH THE COMPETITORS

For each relevant competitor, investigate:

1. Market presence and positioning
   - Target markets and customer segments
   - Market share, revenue, or company size, where reliable data is available
   - Main positioning and reputation

2. Products and services
   - Main offerings
   - Features, variations, and service levels
   - Notable capabilities or limitations

3. Pricing and revenue model
   - Publicly available prices
   - Subscription, one-time, usage-based, or other pricing models
   - Additional products, services, or fees

4. Distribution channels
   - Direct sales, online platforms, retail, partners, or other channels
   - Relevant distribution relationships

5. Marketing and customer acquisition
   - Main marketing messages
   - Visible marketing channels and campaigns
   - Evidence of advertising, content marketing, partnerships, or other acquisition approaches

6. Value proposition and differentiators
   - Main reasons customers may choose the competitor
   - Important competitive advantages
   - Strengths that may be difficult for a new entrant to replicate

7. Customer base
   - Customer industries, company sizes, locations, or other relevant characteristics
   - Demographic information only when supported by credible evidence

8. Customer feedback and reputation
   - Common positive and negative feedback
   - Recurring complaints or unmet needs
   - Potential reasons customers remain with or switch away from the solution

PART 3: RESEARCH SOURCES

Use relevant sources, including:
- Official competitor websites
- Product documentation and pricing pages
- Industry reports and public databases
- Statistics Canada and other government sources
- News articles and company announcements
- Customer review platforms
- Public social media discussions
- Publicly available advertising and promotional materials
- Other credible sources relevant to the market

For every important finding, provide a source link.

Distinguish clearly between:
- Verified facts
- Estimates or interpretations
- Information that could not be verified

Do not invent revenue figures, market share, customer demographics, pricing, or other unavailable information.

If sources conflict, explain the discrepancy.

Consider the publication date of each source and identify information that may be outdated.

Do not treat promotional claims as independently verified facts.

PART 4: COMPETITIVE COMPARISON

Create a comparison table summarizing the most relevant competitors across:
- Target customers
- Main offerings
- Pricing
- Positioning
- Key strengths
- Key weaknesses
- Potential opportunities

PART 5: MARKET OPPORTUNITIES

Conclude with no more than two paragraphs explaining:

1. Where the market appears crowded or where competitors offer similar solutions, pricing, or positioning.
2. Where there may be opportunities to address unmet needs, improve customer experiences, or offer a different approach.

Base your conclusions on the research.

Clearly identify any opportunities that remain hypotheses requiring customer validation.

Present the results in a structured report with tables, concise explanations, and source links.

Important: AI-generated research should be treated as a starting point, not a completed competitive analysis.

AI tools can overlook competitors, misinterpret reviews, use outdated information, or produce unsupported claims.

Verify important findings using original sources and, whenever possible, complement online research with conversations with potential customers.

Avoid uploading confidential company information or personal customer data to AI tools without appropriate authorization and safeguards.

docs.title: Trustpilot / Capterra / G2
docs.text:
Trustpilot, Capterra, and G2 are online review platforms where consumers share experiences with businesses.

You can use them to explore customer feedback, identify recurring complaints, and understand what customers appreciate about competing companies.

Look beyond overall ratings. Read individual reviews, consider their dates, look for consistent themes, and remember that online reviews may not represent the full customer base.

docs.title: BDC - How to conduct a competitive analysis
Asana - How to create a competitive analysis (with examples)
Put it into practice
docs.text:
Create an initial competition analysis for your business idea.

Start by identifying five competitors or alternatives that your potential customers might consider.

Try to include a mix of direct competitors, indirect competitors, and substitutes.

Then:

  1. Research: Visit their websites and review their products, services, pricing, and positioning.
  2. Compare: Create a competitor comparison matrix using the factors most relevant to your market.
  3. Explore feedback: Look for customer reviews and identify recurring strengths, complaints, or unmet needs.
  4. Visualize: Build a perceptual map using two characteristics that matter to your target customers.
  5. Identify opportunities: Write down potential gaps, areas of strong competition, and assumptions you need to investigate further.

You can use the suggested AI prompt to support your research, but make sure you verify the information that influences your conclusions.

Before considering your initial analysis complete, ask yourself:

  • Who are my most relevant direct and indirect competitors?
  • What alternatives are potential customers already using?
  • Why do customers choose these solutions?
  • What do existing competitors do particularly well?
  • What complaints or unmet needs appear repeatedly?
  • Where might my proposed solution offer something different?
  • Which findings are supported by evidence, and which are still assumptions?

Use your findings to prepare a short summary of the competitive landscape and the opportunities you want to investigate.

Your analysis doesn't need to be exhaustive. It should give you a clearer understanding of the market and help you decide what to explore next.

Consider reviewing your findings with your TechAlliance advisor to identify assumptions worth testing during the Discovery stage.

As your business evolves, revisit your analysis to account for new competitors, changing customer needs, and developments in your market.

docs.title: Organize, protect, and preserve your business information
docs.text:
As your business develops, you'll create and collect important information about your customers, products, finances, operations, and decisions.

This information is part of your company's knowledge. Keeping it organized, secure, and accessible to the right people can help you operate more effectively, make informed decisions, and prepare for future opportunities.

A data room is a structured, access-controlled collection of business documents and information. It provides a central place to organize important records and share them with authorized people when needed.

While data rooms are commonly associated with fundraising and investor due diligence, the same principles can help you manage your company's knowledge throughout its development.

You don't need to wait until your business is large or preparing for investment to start organizing its information (and, in fact, it's highly recommended that you don't wait!).

docs.title: Why does it matter?
docs.text:
As your company grows, important knowledge can become scattered across personal computers, email accounts, messaging platforms, and individual team members.

This creates risks. Documents may be lost, information may become outdated, and important decisions or processes may be difficult to understand when someone leaves the company.

Establishing a structured approach to storing business information can help you:

  • Preserve company knowledge: Keep important information available even as team members, roles, and responsibilities change.
  • Protect sensitive information: Reduce the risk of unauthorized access to confidential business, customer, and financial records.
  • Improve collaboration: Help authorized team members find the information they need without relying on individual employees.
  • Support business continuity: Maintain access to essential documents when unexpected changes or disruptions occur.
  • Prepare for opportunities: Organize the information you may need for funding applications, partnerships, audits, or investor due diligence.
  • Make informed decisions: Keep relevant records, plans, and historical information available for future reference.

Your company's knowledge is an important business asset. Protecting and maintaining it should be part of how you operate from the beginning.

docs.title: What information should you organize?
docs.text:
The information you maintain will depend on your business, industry, and stage of development.

Consider organizing your documents into the following categories:

  • Company information: Business plans, incorporation records, ownership information, organizational structure, and strategic documents.
  • Products and technology: Product documentation, technical specifications, architecture diagrams, development roadmaps, and intellectual property records.
  • Market and customers: Market research, customer insights, competitive analysis, and relevant commercial information.
  • Financial information: Financial statements, budgets, projections, revenue reports, and other financial records.
  • Operations and processes: Internal procedures, workflows, policies, supplier information, and operational documentation.
  • People and team: Organizational charts, role descriptions, onboarding materials, and relevant employment documentation.
  • Legal and compliance: Contracts, agreements, licences, policies, and regulatory documentation.
  • Funding and partnerships: Pitch decks, funding applications, investor materials, partnership agreements, and due diligence documents.

Not every category will apply to your business immediately.

Start with the information you already have and identify which documents are essential to your operations.

Some information, such as passwords, credentials, confidential employee records, and sensitive customer data, requires additional protection and should be managed through appropriate dedicated systems rather than ordinary shared folders.

docs.title: Keep your company's knowledge safe
docs.text:
Organizing information is only part of the process. You also need to consider how it's stored, protected, maintained, and accessed.

A shared folder alone doesn't guarantee that your information is secure.

Consider these practices:
