  • Use company-controlled accounts: Store business information in systems managed by your company rather than relying on personal accounts.
  • Control access: Give people access only to the information they need for their responsibilities.
  • Protect accounts: Use strong authentication, including multi-factor authentication (MFA), wherever available.
  • Maintain backups: Keep recoverable copies of important information and periodically test your ability to restore them.
  • Manage permissions: Review who can access, edit, download, or share documents, especially when team members or external collaborators change.
  • Keep information current: Establish a process for reviewing and updating important documents.
  • Track document changes: Use version history or document management practices to reduce confusion and preserve important revisions.
  • Protect confidential information: Apply appropriate safeguards to customer data, intellectual property, financial records, and other sensitive materials.
  • Plan for continuity: Make sure essential company knowledge remains accessible to authorized people if a team member becomes unavailable or leaves.

For sensitive information, consider whether your storage platform provides the security controls, data protection features, and access management your business requires.

Depending on the type of information you handle, additional legal, privacy, contractual, or regulatory requirements may apply.

docs.title: Knowledge management structure
docs.text:
A knowledge management structure helps you decide how information should be organized, maintained, and accessed within your company.

Start by identifying the main categories of information your business creates and uses.

For each category, consider:

  • Purpose: Why does your business need this information?
  • Location: Where should it be stored?
  • Ownership: Who is responsible for maintaining it?
  • Access: Who should be allowed to view or modify it?
  • Maintenance: How often should it be reviewed or updated?
  • Retention: How long should it be kept, and when should it be securely archived or deleted?

This approach helps establish clear responsibilities and reduces the risk of important knowledge becoming disorganized or dependent on one person.

docs.title: Document management checklist
docs.text:
A document management checklist can help you assess whether your company's important records are organized and protected.

For each document or group of documents, track:

  • Document name and category
  • Storage location
  • Responsible team member
  • Last review or update
  • Access permissions
  • Confidentiality or sensitivity level
  • Backup and recovery arrangements

Use the checklist to identify missing documents, outdated information, unnecessary access permissions, or other areas that need attention.

docs.title: Investor and partner data room
docs.text:
When preparing for fundraising, partnerships, or due diligence, you may need to share selected company information with external parties.

Instead of granting access to your entire internal document library, create a separate data room containing only the information relevant to that specific request.

For example, an investor data room may include:

  • Company overview and pitch deck
  • Business model and market analysis
  • Product information and development roadmap
  • Financial statements and projections
  • Customer traction and business metrics
  • Ownership structure and capitalization table
  • Relevant contracts and legal documents
  • Funding requirements and proposed use of funds

The documents required will depend on the purpose and stage of the discussion.

Keep your internal knowledge repository separate from external data rooms. This allows you to maintain your company's information while controlling what you share with investors, partners, or other third parties.

Review confidentiality requirements and access permissions before sharing sensitive documents.

docs.title: Google Drive
docs.text:
Google Drive is a cloud storage and file-sharing platform that can help you organize documents, collaborate with team members, and manage access to business information.

You can create folders, share documents, and maintain version history for supported files.

For company knowledge management, consider using an appropriate Google Workspace setup with organization-managed accounts and shared storage rather than relying on an individual's personal account.

Review your storage, sharing, and security settings before using it for sensitive business information.

docs.title: Microsoft OneDrive
docs.text:
Microsoft OneDrive provides cloud storage and file-sharing capabilities, with integration into Microsoft 365 applications such as Word, Excel, and PowerPoint.

It can help team members store and work with business documents while maintaining access across devices.

For company-wide knowledge, consider how OneDrive fits into your organization's broader document management approach, including shared ownership, access permissions, and employee transitions.

docs.title: Microsoft SharePoint
docs.text:
Microsoft SharePoint is a document management and collaboration platform designed to help organizations organize and share information.

It supports document libraries, permissions, version history, and collaboration across teams.

SharePoint can be useful for businesses that need structured, company-managed document storage with multiple contributors and different access requirements.

Its available features and security controls depend on your Microsoft 365 configuration and subscription.

docs.title: Reference sources
docs.text: The following resources focus primarily on preparing data rooms for investors. They can also help you understand how to organize business documents and prepare information for external review.

docs.title: MaRS - Data room basics for startups: Stage 1 data for the term sheet
Pageform - Step-by-step guide to building an investor data room
TechAlliance MasterClass - Building Your Data Room
Put it into practice
docs.text:
Create a basic, company-controlled document repository where you can organize and maintain your business information.

Start with a simple folder structure:

  1. Company information
  2. Products and technology
  3. Market and customers
  4. Financial information
  5. Operations and processes
  6. People and team
  7. Legal and compliance
  8. Funding and partnerships

Adjust these categories to match your business. You don't need to create every folder or prepare every document immediately.

Once you've established your structure:

  1. Organize: Identify your existing business documents and move them into appropriate company-managed storage.
  2. Review: Check that important documents are accurate, clearly named, and up to date.
  3. Protect: Review access permissions, enable available security protections, and identify information that requires more secure storage.
  4. Assign ownership: Decide who will maintain each category of information.
  5. Plan for recovery: Confirm that important information is backed up and can be restored if needed.
  6. Maintain: Establish a simple process for reviewing and updating your company's knowledge as the business evolves.

Before considering your initial setup complete, ask yourself:

  • Can authorized team members find the information they need?
  • Is important business knowledge stored in company-controlled systems?
  • Could the business access essential information if a team member left unexpectedly?
  • Are confidential documents protected from unnecessary access?
  • Do we have a reliable way to recover important information if it's lost or deleted?
  • Do we know who is responsible for keeping our documents current?

You don't need a complex system to get started. Focus on creating a structure that's practical for your business and can evolve as your needs change.

Consider discussing your document management approach, security concerns, and information-sharing needs with your TechAlliance advisor.

docs.title: Explain your business clearly, wherever the conversation takes you
docs.text:
You have an idea for a business, product, or service. But can you explain it to someone who's hearing about it for the first time?

An elevator pitch is a short, clear introduction to your business or idea. It helps someone quickly understand what you're working on, who it's for, and why it matters.

The name comes from the idea of explaining your business during a short elevator ride. In practice, you might use your pitch at a networking event, during a customer conversation, in a meeting with a potential investor, or when introducing yourself to someone new.

A good elevator pitch doesn't need to explain everything about your business. Its purpose is to communicate the most relevant information, create interest, and open the door to a more detailed conversation.

docs.title: One business, different pitches
docs.text:
You shouldn't rely on a single elevator pitch for every situation.

Different audiences care about different things. A potential customer wants to understand how your solution could help them. An investor may be more interested in your market opportunity, business model, and growth potential.

Your core message should remain consistent, but what you emphasize should change depending on who you're speaking with and what you hope to achieve.

Consider preparing different versions for these situations:

  • General introduction: Explain what your business does, who it serves, and the problem you're working to solve. Keep it simple enough for someone unfamiliar with your industry.
  • Potential customer: Focus on the customer's problem, how your solution addresses it, and the value it could provide. Your goal may be to understand their needs or arrange a follow-up conversation.
  • Potential investor: Highlight the market opportunity, your proposed solution, business model, and any evidence of traction you have. Explain what you're looking for and why the opportunity may be worth exploring.
  • Potential partner: Explain what your business does, how your work relates to theirs, and where a collaboration might create value.
  • Potential team member: Communicate the problem you're working on, your vision for the business, and why someone might want to contribute.

You may also need shorter or longer versions depending on the situation.

For example, a brief introduction at a networking event might take 15 to 30 seconds, while a conversation with an interested investor or partner may allow more time.

The goal is to have a clear message you can adapt naturally, rather than memorizing a script for every possible situation.

docs.title: What makes an effective elevator pitch?
docs.text:
Regardless of your audience, a strong elevator pitch should be:

  • Clear: Use language your listener can understand, even if they're unfamiliar with your industry.
  • Concise: Focus on the information that matters most. Save technical details and background information for follow-up questions.
  • Relevant: Connect your message to the interests, challenges, or goals of the person you're speaking with.
  • Specific: Explain the problem and your proposed solution using concrete details rather than broad claims.
  • Credible: Support your message with real information. Don't exaggerate your progress, results, or capabilities.
  • Action-oriented: Know what you'd like to happen next, whether that's getting feedback, arranging a meeting, or continuing the conversation.

Avoid relying on buzzwords, technical jargon, or claims that are difficult to support.

If your business is still at the idea stage, be clear about what you're exploring rather than presenting assumptions as proven facts.

docs.title: Founder Institute elevator pitch framework
docs.text:
The Founder Institute provides a simple framework for organizing a startup elevator pitch around four questions:

  1. What are you building? Explain your business or idea and the problem it aims to solve.
  2. Why now? Describe why the opportunity is relevant and what makes the timing important.
  3. Why you? Explain what makes you or your team suited to pursue the opportunity.
  4. What's your ask? Clarify what you're looking for from the conversation.

This framework can be particularly useful when introducing your business to investors, potential partners, or others interested in the opportunity behind your idea.

You don't need to include every element in every conversation. Adapt the framework to your audience and the time available.

docs.title: Audience-specific pitch framework
docs.text:
Use this simple exercise to develop different versions of your pitch.

Before writing, answer four questions:

  1. Who am I speaking with? Identify your audience and what they may care about.
  2. What do they need to understand? Choose the most relevant information about your business.
  3. Why should it matter to them? Connect your idea or solution to their interests or needs.
  4. What do I want to happen next? Identify a reasonable next step for the conversation.

Then build your pitch around those answers.

For example:

General introduction

"We're developing [product or service] to help [target audience] address [specific problem]. Our approach focuses on [main benefit or difference]."

Potential customer

"We're working with [target audience] who experience [specific problem]. Our proposed solution helps them [desired outcome]. I'd be interested in learning how you're currently handling this challenge."

Potential investor

"We're building [solution] for [target market] to address [problem]. We see an opportunity because [market insight or evidence]. We've achieved [verified progress, if available], and we're currently looking for [specific next step]."

These are starting points, not scripts you need to follow word for word.

Adjust the language to reflect your business, your current stage, and the person you're speaking with.

docs.title: Pitch feedback and refinement
docs.text:
Your first version probably won't be your final version.

Practise explaining your business to people with different levels of familiarity with your industry.

After each conversation, consider:

  • Did the person understand what my business does?
  • Which parts of my explanation needed clarification?
  • What questions did they ask?
  • Did I focus on information relevant to them?
  • Was the next step clear?

Use their reactions and questions to improve your message.

A pitch should evolve as you learn more about your customers, refine your solution, and gather evidence about your business opportunity.

docs.title: Google Docs
docs.text:
Google Docs is a collaborative writing tool you can use to draft, organize, and refine different versions of your elevator pitch.

Consider creating a single document with sections for general introductions, customer conversations, investor discussions, and partnership opportunities.

You can also share your drafts with trusted advisors or collaborators to collect feedback.

docs.title: Microsoft Word
docs.text:
Microsoft Word can help you write, edit, and organize your pitches in one place.

Use separate sections for different audiences, track revisions, and add notes about questions or feedback you receive during conversations.

docs.title: Loom
docs.text:
Loom is a video recording and sharing platform that can help you practise delivering your pitch.

Record yourself explaining your business, then review the recording to evaluate your clarity, pace, and delivery.

You can also share recordings with trusted contacts to gather feedback.

Review the platform's current features and privacy settings before recording or sharing sensitive business information.

docs.title: BDC - How to write an elevator pitch
Founder Institute - Perfecting your elevator pitch
Put it into practice
docs.text:
Create three versions of your elevator pitch for different situations.

Start by writing a general introduction to your business.

Try to explain your idea in approximately 30 seconds, covering:

  • Who you are and what you're working on
  • Who your business aims to serve
  • What problem you're trying to solve
  • How your proposed solution addresses that problem

Once you have a clear general introduction, adapt it for two additional audiences.

For example:

  1. General introduction: Prepare a version you could use when meeting someone at a networking event.
  2. Potential customer: Prepare a version that emphasizes the customer's problem and opens the door to learning more about their needs.
  3. Potential investor: Prepare a version that highlights the business opportunity, your approach, and what you're hoping to achieve.

You can choose other audiences if they're more relevant to your current goals.

Next, practise your pitches.

Say each version out loud and check whether it sounds natural. Try recording yourself or presenting it to someone unfamiliar with your business.

Pay attention to:

  • Clarity: Can someone understand your idea without additional explanation?
  • Length: Can you communicate the essential information without rushing?
  • Relevance: Does each version focus on what matters to its intended audience?
  • Confidence: Can you explain your idea naturally without reading a script?
  • Next steps: Does your pitch make it easy to continue the conversation?

Ask for feedback, make adjustments, and practise again.

Before considering your pitches ready, ask yourself:

  • Can I explain my business to someone with no technical background?
  • Do I know which details matter most to customers, investors, and partners?
  • Am I making claims I can support with evidence?
  • Can I adjust my pitch when someone asks an unexpected question?
  • Do I know what I want to achieve from each conversation?

Your elevator pitch will change as your business develops. Keep your different versions accessible, revisit them as you learn, and update them when your business direction or priorities change.

Consider practising your pitches with your TechAlliance advisor to identify opportunities to make your message clearer and more relevant to each audience.

docs.title: Is it worth it?
docs.text:
Your business might still be an idea. You may not have customers, investors, or employees yet. But taking time to plan can help you understand what you're building, why it matters, and what you need to do next.

A business plan helps you organize your priorities, identify gaps in your knowledge, and determine where you may need additional support. It also gives you a starting point for testing assumptions, exploring opportunities, and making informed decisions as your idea develops.

Planning becomes especially important when seeking funding. For example, banks and other lenders may request a business plan to better understand your goals, financial projections, and how you intend to achieve them.

Your plan can also guide decisions across your business, from the processes you establish to the people you hire. Consider two manufacturers: one aims to offer the lowest prices in its market, while the other focuses on delivering premium quality. Their priorities will influence everything from equipment purchases to staffing and production processes.

The good news is that you don't need a lengthy, traditional business plan to get started.

For early-stage technology ventures, simpler planning tools can help you explore your business model without spending weeks preparing a detailed document.

One widely used approach is the Business Model Canvas, developed by Alexander Osterwalder and Yves Pigneur. It provides a visual framework for exploring how a business creates, delivers, and captures value.

Your initial plan doesn't need to be perfect or permanent. It will likely change as you learn more about your customers, test your assumptions, and refine your solution.

What matters is having a clear starting point. A simple plan can help you identify potential customers, define what you intend to offer, and explore how your business might generate revenue.

Ready to explore the tools?

docs.title: Business Model Canvas (BMC)
docs.text:
Developed by Alexander Osterwalder and introduced in his earlier research before being popularized through the 2010 book Business Model Generation, co-authored with Yves Pigneur, the Business Model Canvas is a widely used tool for exploring and designing business models.

It organizes nine key elements of a business on a single page, helping you see how different parts of your business connect.

The canvas can help you explore your customers, value proposition, revenue streams, costs, and other important elements without creating a lengthy business plan.

docs.title: Lean Canvas
docs.text:
Created by Ash Maurya, the Lean Canvas adapts the Business Model Canvas with a stronger focus on the challenges and uncertainties faced by early-stage businesses.

It emphasizes areas such as customer problems, proposed solutions, key metrics, and competitive advantages.

The Lean Canvas can be particularly useful when you're still exploring your idea and need to identify which assumptions to test before investing significant resources.

Like the Business Model Canvas, it provides a simple, visual way to organize your thinking and update your approach as you learn.

docs.title: Project Premortem
docs.text:
A project premortem is a planning exercise that helps you identify potential risks before they become real problems.

Imagine you're looking back at your business six months or a year from now, and things haven't gone as planned. Your venture has failed, or you've fallen significantly short of your goals.

What might have gone wrong?

List realistic reasons for that outcome, then consider what you could do today to reduce the likelihood of those problems occurring.

This exercise can help you challenge assumptions, recognize potential obstacles, and prepare for risks you might otherwise overlook.

docs.title: Canvanizer
docs.text:
An online tool for creating and working with visual business canvases, including the Business Model Canvas and Lean Canvas.

Canvanizer offers options for organizing ideas, collaborating, and exporting your work. Check its current plans and features to find the option that meets your needs.

docs.title: Miro
docs.text:
A collaborative digital whiteboard that helps you organize ideas, map processes, and work with others.

Miro offers templates for business planning, including the Business Model Canvas, Lean Canvas, and premortem exercises. A free plan is available, with limitations depending on the features you need.

docs.title: Miro - Lean Canvas vs. Business Model Canvas
Put it into practice
docs.text:
Choose the Business Model Canvas or Lean Canvas and try completing a first draft for your idea.

Focus on what you currently know, and make note of any assumptions or questions that still need answers.

You don't need to fill in every section perfectly. Use the canvas to organize your thinking and identify what you should explore next.

Consider sharing your draft with your TechAlliance advisor to discuss your assumptions and priorities.

docs.title: Find out who might need your solution
docs.text:
You have an idea for a product or service. But who would actually benefit from it, and who might be willing to pay for it?

Understanding your potential customers is an important step in exploring a business opportunity.

A customer segment is a group of people or organizations that share characteristics, needs, behaviours, or challenges relevant to your business.

Different groups may experience the same problem in different ways. They may also have different budgets, priorities, purchasing habits, and expectations.

For example, a software solution designed to improve scheduling could serve independent professionals, small businesses, and large organizations. Although these customers may share a similar challenge, their requirements and purchasing decisions could be very different.

Rather than trying to serve everyone, start by identifying the groups most likely to benefit from your proposed solution.

The goal is to understand where your idea might create value and which potential customers are worth learning more about.

docs.title: Understand the different types of customers
docs.text:
The way you research potential customers depends partly on how your business intends to sell its products or services.

Consider these common business models:

  • Business-to-consumer (B2C): You sell directly to individual customers. Relevant characteristics may include location, lifestyle, purchasing habits, needs, and spending priorities.
  • Business-to-business (B2B): You sell to other companies or organizations. Relevant characteristics may include industry, company size, location, operational challenges, and purchasing processes.
  • Business-to-business-to-consumer (B2B2C): You reach end customers through another business or platform. You'll need to understand both the organizations you work with and the people who ultimately use or purchase your solution.

Some businesses serve more than one type of customer.

For example, a technology company might sell software directly to organizations while also offering a version for individual users.

Understanding these differences helps you decide what information to research and which potential customers to prioritize.

docs.title: What makes a useful customer segment?
docs.text:
A useful customer segment is more specific than a broad category such as "small businesses" or "people who use technology."

Consider the characteristics that could influence whether someone needs, chooses, or pays for your solution.

For B2B customers, explore:

  • Industry or business sector
  • Company size and stage of development
  • Geographic location
  • Department or team experiencing the problem
  • Decision-makers and people involved in purchasing
  • Existing tools, processes, or alternatives
  • Budget and purchasing requirements
  • Urgency and impact of the problem

For B2C customers, explore:

  • Geographic location
  • Relevant demographic characteristics
  • Needs, interests, and behaviours
  • Purchasing and consumption habits
  • Current solutions or alternatives
  • Spending patterns and price sensitivity
  • Frequency and urgency of the problem
  • Where they discover, evaluate, and purchase products

Not every characteristic will matter equally.

For example, age may be relevant for some consumer products but much less useful than purchasing behaviour or the specific problem a customer experiences.

Focus on characteristics that help you understand customer needs and purchasing decisions.

docs.title: Research supply and demand
docs.text:
Before choosing a customer segment, explore what is already available in your target market and whether there are signs of demand for your proposed solution.

Supply refers to the products, services, and alternatives currently available to customers.

Demand refers to the interest, need, and willingness to obtain or pay for a solution.

Start by asking:

  • What products or services are already available in the market?
  • Who currently provides them?
  • Are people searching for solutions to the problem?
  • Are there reports or studies about relevant purchasing behaviours?
  • What alternatives are customers currently using?
  • Are there indications that some customer groups are underserved?
  • Are there geographic markets where the problem may be more relevant?

Online search activity, industry reports, customer reviews, and competitor information can provide useful signals.

However, search interest doesn't automatically mean purchase demand.

People may search for information without intending to buy anything. Likewise, a problem may exist even when customers aren't searching for a specific product category.

Use market research to identify potential opportunities, then investigate those opportunities through customer conversations and other validation activities.

docs.title: Identify your potential early adopters
docs.text:
Not every customer will be equally interested in trying a new solution.

Early adopters are customers who may be more willing to explore a new product or service because they recognize the problem and have a strong reason to address it.

They may already be looking for alternatives, spending money on imperfect solutions, or investing significant time in workarounds.

When considering potential early adopters, ask:

  • Who experiences the problem most frequently or intensely?
  • Who is already trying to solve it?
  • Who has the resources or authority to act?
  • Who would benefit most from a better approach?
  • Who might be willing to try an early version of the solution?

At the Idea stage, your early adopter segment is still a hypothesis.

You may have a strong initial guess, but you'll need customer discovery and validation to understand whether that group is genuinely interested.

docs.title: Customer segmentation matrix
docs.text:
A customer segmentation matrix helps you compare potential customer groups and decide which ones deserve further research.

Start by identifying three to five customer segments that might benefit from your solution.

Then compare them using criteria relevant to your business.

Criteria Segment A Segment B Segment C Customer description Main problem Current alternatives Problem frequency or urgency Potential willingness to pay Geographic market Ease of reaching customers Evidence of demand

Use the matrix to identify which segments appear most promising.

Clearly distinguish between findings supported by research and assumptions that still need validation.

docs.title: TAM, SAM, and SOM
docs.text:
TAM, SAM, and SOM are market-sizing concepts that help you understand the potential scale of a business opportunity.

  • Total Addressable Market (TAM): The total market demand for a product or service if you could serve everyone within the defined market.
  • Serviceable Available Market (SAM): The portion of that market your business could realistically serve based on its offering, geography, and business model.
  • Serviceable Obtainable Market (SOM): The portion of the serviceable market your business could reasonably aim to capture within a defined period.

These estimates can help you understand whether a potential customer segment represents a meaningful opportunity.

Avoid relying on broad industry figures without considering whether the customers included are relevant to your specific solution.

For an early-stage venture, a smaller, clearly defined market estimate supported by reasonable assumptions may be more useful than a large figure with little connection to your target customers.

docs.title: Ideal customer profile (ICP)
docs.text:
An ideal customer profile describes the characteristics of the customer or organization most likely to benefit from your solution.

For a B2B business, an ICP might include:

  • Industry
  • Company size
  • Geographic location
  • Relevant department
  • Operational challenge
  • Existing solutions
  • Purchasing requirements

For a B2C business, it may focus more on needs, behaviours, circumstances, and purchasing motivations.

Your initial ICP should be treated as a working hypothesis.

As you speak with potential customers, you can refine it based on what you learn about their problems, priorities, and willingness to act.

docs.title: Early adopter hypothesis
docs.text:
Use this simple framework to describe who you believe might adopt your solution first.

"We believe [SPECIFIC CUSTOMER SEGMENT] experiences [PROBLEM] and currently addresses it through [EXISTING SOLUTION OR WORKAROUND].

We believe this group may be interested in a new solution because [REASON OR EVIDENCE].

We need to investigate [MAIN ASSUMPTIONS] before deciding whether to focus on this segment."

This statement helps turn broad market research into a clear hypothesis you can test during customer discovery.

docs.title: ChatGPT / Claude / DeepSeek / Augure[1]
docs.text:
"Traditional" LLM tools can help you research what is available; they can also help you identify industry reports, demographic information, market trends, and potential sources of demand.

Use the suggested research prompt below to organize your investigation.

[1]: Augure is the only fully Canadian option from this list

docs.title: Perplexity
docs.text:
Perplexity is an AI-powered research and search tool that can help you investigate customer groups, discover relevant market information, and locate supporting sources.

It may be useful for exploring unfamiliar industries, identifying market trends, and finding public reports about purchasing behaviours or customer needs.

Review original sources before relying on important findings.

docs.title: Suggested AI research prompt
docs.text:
Use the following prompt with an AI research tool that supports web searches.

Replace the information in brackets with details about your business.

Act as an experienced business development and market research analyst specializing in customer segmentation for startups.

I'm exploring a venture called [VENTURE NAME].

Website (if available): [WEBSITE URL]
Proposed products or services: [DESCRIPTION]
Business location: [CITY, PROVINCE/STATE, COUNTRY]
Initial target markets: [GEOGRAPHIC MARKETS OR ONLINE]
Business model: [B2B, B2C, B2B2C, OR UNKNOWN]
Problem we aim to solve: [CUSTOMER PROBLEM]

I need you to research potential customer segments, assess available evidence of demand, and identify which groups may be worth investigating first.

Use credible, publicly available sources and provide links to support important findings.

PART 1: RESEARCH THE INITIAL MARKET

Investigate the proposed products or services within my initial target market.

Research:

1. Existing supply
   - What comparable products, services, and alternatives are available?
   - Which types of providers serve the market?
   - Are there signs of a crowded or underserved market?

2. Potential demand
   - What evidence exists of customer interest or demand?
   - Are people searching for these products or the problems they address?
   - Are there relevant purchasing, usage, or consumption trends?
   - What credible reports, statistics, or studies describe the market?

Distinguish between evidence of interest, evidence of purchasing behaviour, and evidence of willingness to pay.

Do not assume search volume alone proves demand.

PART 2: IDENTIFY POTENTIAL CUSTOMER SEGMENTS

Identify customer groups that may benefit from the proposed solution.

For B2B opportunities, investigate:
- Relevant industries or business sectors
- Company size and stage
- Geographic concentration
- Departments or teams experiencing the problem
- Potential decision-makers and purchasing stakeholders
- Main customer problems
- Existing solutions and workarounds
- Available evidence of spending or purchasing behaviour
- Potential market size

For B2C opportunities, investigate:
- Relevant demographic and behavioural characteristics
- Geographic concentration
- Customer needs and motivations
- Main customer problems
- Existing solutions and workarounds
- Available evidence of spending or purchasing behaviour
- Potential market size

For B2B2C opportunities, also investigate:
- Potential intermediary businesses or platforms
- Where end customers currently discover or purchase alternatives
- How the needs of intermediary businesses differ from those of end customers

Only include demographic characteristics that are relevant to the product or purchasing decision.

PART 3: EXPLORE ALTERNATIVE MARKETS

If evidence of demand in the initial market is limited, investigate other potential geographic markets.

Consider relevant locations within:
- Canada
- North America
- Other international markets, when appropriate

Research:
- Where people or organizations appear to experience the problem
- Where relevant products or alternatives are being searched for or purchased
- Whether competing solutions already serve those markets
- Comparable geographic markets with similar customer characteristics
- Potential barriers to entering those markets

Do not conclude that a market has no demand simply because public search or market data is limited.

Explain the evidence and limitations behind each recommendation.

PART 4: ESTIMATE MARKET SIZE

Where credible data is available, estimate the potential market size for relevant customer segments.

Consider:
- Total Addressable Market (TAM)
- Serviceable Available Market (SAM)
- Serviceable Obtainable Market (SOM), when reasonable assumptions are available

Explain:
- The data sources used
- The calculation method
- Important assumptions
- Geographic and customer segment boundaries
- Limitations or uncertainty

Do not invent market size figures or present unsupported estimates as verified facts.

PART 5: IDENTIFY POTENTIAL EARLY ADOPTERS

Compare the most promising customer segments based on:
- Problem urgency or frequency
- Existing spending or effort to solve the problem
- Evidence of demand
- Potential willingness and ability to pay
- Ease of reaching the customer group
- Competitive alternatives
- Potential barriers to adoption

Recommend one segment as the strongest initial early adopter hypothesis.

Explain why this group appears promising and what evidence would be needed to validate the recommendation.

Do not present the recommendation as a confirmed customer segment.

PART 6: RESEARCH SOURCES

Use relevant and credible sources, including:
- Statistics Canada and other government databases
- Industry and market research reports
- Official economic and demographic data
- News articles and credible industry publications
- Public customer reviews and discussions
- Competitor websites and pricing information
- Google Trends and other search trend platforms
- Publicly available competitive intelligence tools
- Other relevant sources

For important findings, provide source links.

Distinguish between:
- Verified facts
- Estimates or interpretations
- Assumptions requiring validation
- Information that could not be verified

Consider the publication dates and limitations of sources.

Do not invent customer demographics, purchasing behaviour, search volume, market size, or other unavailable information.

PART 7: FINAL OUTPUT

Present:
1. A brief overview of supply and demand in the initial market
2. A comparison table of potential customer segments
3. Relevant geographic market opportunities
4. Market size estimates, where supported
5. A recommended early adopter hypothesis
6. The most important assumptions to test through customer discovery
7. Source links for important findings

Conclude with no more than two paragraphs summarizing the most promising customer segments, relevant geographic markets, and recommended early adopter hypothesis.

Keep conclusions practical, evidence-based, and clear about uncertainty.

Important: AI-assisted market research can help you identify potential opportunities, but it cannot confirm that customers need or will purchase your solution.

AI tools may rely on incomplete data, outdated reports, or assumptions that don't reflect your specific market.

Verify important findings using original sources and use customer conversations to investigate whether your proposed segments experience the problem you're trying to solve.

Avoid sharing confidential business information or personal customer data with AI tools without appropriate authorization and safeguards.

docs.title: Statistics Canada
docs.text:
Statistics Canada provides official data about Canada's population, businesses, industries, economy, and other topics.

You can use its data to investigate demographic characteristics, business populations, geographic markets, and other factors relevant to your customer segments.

Look for datasets that closely match your target customers rather than relying only on broad national statistics.

docs.title: Google Trends
docs.text:
Google Trends helps you explore relative search interest for topics and search terms across locations and time periods.

It can be useful for comparing interest in different problems, products, or markets.

Remember that Google Trends shows normalized search interest, not total demand or confirmed purchasing behaviour.

docs.title: Google Keyword Planner
docs.text:
Google Keyword Planner can help you explore keywords associated with your product, service, or the problem you're trying to solve.

It provides keyword ideas and search-related estimates that may help you understand how people look for relevant solutions.

Access and available data may depend on your Google Ads account and settings.

Use keyword information as one research signal rather than proof of customer demand.

docs.title: Put it into practice
docs.text:
Identify three potential customer segments for your business idea.

Start by describing the problem your solution aims to address.

Then consider who might experience that problem and how their needs could differ.

For each potential segment:

  1. Describe: Define the customer group using relevant characteristics such as industry, business size, geography, behaviours, or needs.
  2. Research: Look for credible information about the segment, including its size, relevant trends, and existing solutions.
  3. Understand alternatives: Identify how these customers currently address the problem.
  4. Explore demand: Look for evidence that the problem matters and that customers may be willing to invest time or money in solving it.
  5. Compare: Use a customer segmentation matrix to assess which groups appear most promising.

Once you've compared your segments, select one as your initial early adopter hypothesis.

Write a short statement explaining:

  • Who the potential early adopters are
  • What problem you believe they experience
  • How they're currently addressing it
  • Why they might be interested in a different solution
  • What you still need to learn

Before moving forward, ask yourself:

  • Have I defined customer groups that are specific enough to research?
  • What evidence suggests these customers experience the problem?
  • Am I confusing general market interest with actual demand?
  • Do I understand how these customers currently solve the problem?
  • Which segment appears most promising, and why?
  • What assumptions still need to be tested through customer conversations?

Your initial customer segments don't need to be perfect. They're a starting point for learning more about your market.

Consider reviewing your findings and early adopter hypothesis with your TechAlliance advisor before moving into customer discovery.

The next step is to speak with potential customers, understand their experiences, and investigate whether the problem you've identified is important enough for them to address.

docs.title: Grow your business and explore new opportunities
docs.text:
You've developed your solution, built your business foundations, and started establishing how your company operates. Now it's time to explore what comes next.

The Scale stage helps you navigate the challenges and opportunities that come with growing a business, from reaching new customers and expanding into new markets to strengthening your team and managing increasing demand.

Growth brings new decisions, responsibilities, and challenges. This is your opportunity to build on what you've achieved, identify new opportunities, and prepare your business for its next stage.

docs.title: What you'll explore
docs.text:
The resources in this section can help you:

  • Develop your growth strategy: Explore approaches to setting growth goals, identifying opportunities, and planning your next steps.
  • Expand your market reach: Learn about reaching new customers, entering new markets, and developing strategies to increase sales.
  • Strengthen your team and leadership: Explore hiring, leadership development, delegation, and organizational structures that support a growing business.
  • Access capital for growth: Understand different funding and investment options and how they may support your expansion plans.
  • Scale your operations: Explore ways to improve processes, systems, and infrastructure to manage increasing demand.
  • Build strategic partnerships: Identify opportunities to collaborate with other businesses, industry experts, and partners.
  • Measure your performance: Learn how to track key business metrics, evaluate progress, and make informed decisions as your company grows.

docs.title: How to use these resources
docs.text:
Explore the topics available in this section to better understand the opportunities and challenges involved in scaling your business.

Each topic may include practical notes, tools, templates, or links to additional reading that can help you evaluate growth opportunities, develop strategies, and strengthen your business.

If your TechAlliance advisor has recommended specific resources, start there. You can return to other topics as your business goals and priorities evolve.

docs.title: Questions to consider
docs.text:
As you plan for growth, think about:

  • What are my most important growth goals, and how will I measure progress?
  • What opportunities exist to reach new customers or enter new markets?
  • Can my current operations, systems, and processes support increased demand?
  • What skills, leadership capabilities, or additional team members will I need?
  • What financial resources will support my growth plans?
  • What partnerships or connections could help my business expand?
  • What risks or challenges should I prepare for as my business grows?

Use these questions to evaluate your readiness for growth, identify areas that need attention, and prepare for conversations with your TechAlliance advisor.

docs.title: Your next step
docs.text:
Start with the topic that addresses your most important growth opportunity or challenge.

Use what you learn to strengthen your growth strategy, make informed decisions, and build a business that can adapt, compete, and succeed as it expands.

docs.title: Test your solution and build confidence in your next steps
docs.text:
You've explored your idea and learned more about your potential customers. Now it's time to test whether your proposed solution addresses a real need and whether customers see enough value in it to take action.

The Validation stage helps you move from assumptions to evidence by testing your ideas, gathering feedback, and understanding what works, what needs improvement, and what may need to change.

You don't need a fully developed product to get started. This is your opportunity to experiment, learn from real customer interactions, and make more informed decisions about your next steps.

docs.title: What you'll explore
docs.text:
The resources in this section can help you:

  • Test your assumptions: Identify the key beliefs behind your business idea and explore ways to test them.
  • Develop and test your solution: Learn how prototypes, minimum viable products (MVPs), and early experiments can help you evaluate your approach.
  • Gather customer feedback: Understand how potential customers respond to your solution and what their experiences can tell you.
  • Evaluate customer interest: Explore ways to assess demand, willingness to pay, and early signs of customer traction.
  • Refine your approach: Use the evidence you collect to improve your solution, revisit assumptions, or consider a different direction.

docs.title: How to use these resources
docs.text:
Explore the topics available in this section to understand different approaches to testing your solution and evaluating its potential.

Each topic may include practical notes, tools, templates, or links to additional reading that can help you design experiments, collect feedback, and assess your findings.

If your TechAlliance advisor has recommended specific resources, start there. You can return to other topics as your questions and priorities evolve.

docs.title: Questions to consider
docs.text:
As you test your solution, think about:

  • What assumptions do I need to test before moving forward?
  • What's the simplest way to test whether my solution addresses a real customer need?
  • How are potential customers responding to my solution?
  • What evidence do I have that customers are interested or willing to pay?
  • What have I learned from my experiments and customer feedback?
  • What should I improve, change, or investigate further?

Use these questions to evaluate your progress, identify gaps in your evidence, and prepare for conversations with your TechAlliance advisor.

docs.title: Your next step
docs.text:
Start with the topic that helps you test your most important assumption or answer a key question about your solution.

Use what you learn to refine your approach, build confidence in your decisions, and identify what your business needs to move toward greater efficiency and sustainable growth.

docs.title: Test your solution, measure results, and decide what comes next
docs.text:
You've defined your minimum viable product (MVP) or pilot, identified the customers you want to serve, and started gathering feedback through solution interviews.

Now it's time to manage your test in a real-world environment.

MVP and pilot testing is the process of delivering your initial offering to a defined group of customers, observing how they use it, measuring the value it creates, and using the results to guide your next decisions.

This goes beyond asking customers what they think about your solution.

You want to understand what happens when they use it over time.

Do they return? Does it solve their problem? Are they willing to pay? Can your team deliver the experience reliably?

The goal is to gather evidence that helps you decide whether to:

  • Persevere: Continue with your current direction because the evidence supports it.
  • Iterate: Improve specific parts of your offering based on what you've learned.
  • Pivot: Make a meaningful change to your approach because important assumptions aren't holding up.

A successful test isn't necessarily one where everything works. It's one that helps you make a better-informed business decision.

docs.title: Start with a clear testing plan
docs.text:
Before inviting participants to use your MVP or begin a pilot, revisit your MVP/Pilot definition.

You should already have an initial understanding of:

  • The customer problem you're addressing
  • Your target customer segment
  • The product or service you're offering
  • The essential features or activities included
  • The number of participants you want to involve
  • Whether participation is free, discounted, or paid
  • The duration of the test
  • The outcomes you want to achieve

Turn these decisions into a practical testing plan.

Identify who will manage the pilot, who will support participants, how you'll collect data, and when you'll review results.

Make sure participants understand what they're receiving, what is expected of them, and how the test will work.

If your solution involves sensitive information, physical safety, regulated activities, or other significant risks, address the relevant requirements before testing begins.

You may also need agreements covering participation, confidentiality, data handling, responsibilities, or payment.

docs.title: Measure what matters to your customers
docs.text:
It's easy to focus on numbers that look encouraging but don't tell you whether your solution works.

For example, having 100 people register for a product doesn't necessarily mean those people are receiving value.

Instead, focus on metrics connected to the problem you're trying to solve.

If your product is designed to save time, measure whether customers actually save time.

If it's designed to simplify a process, observe whether customers can complete that process more easily.

If it's designed to improve business performance, identify which outcomes you can reasonably measure during the test.

Consider four categories of evidence.

docs.title: 1. Product usage and engagement
docs.text:
These metrics help you understand whether participants are using your offering.

Examples include:

  • Activation rate: The percentage of participants who complete a meaningful first action.
  • Feature adoption: The percentage of relevant participants who use a particular feature.
  • Usage frequency: How often participants use the product or service.
  • Task completion rate: The percentage of attempts in which participants successfully complete a defined task.
  • Retention: The percentage of participants who continue using the offering over a defined period.

Choose metrics that reflect how your solution is intended to be used.

A product designed for daily use should be evaluated differently from a service customers need only once a month.

docs.title: 2. Customer outcomes
docs.text:
These metrics help you determine whether your solution delivers meaningful value.

Examples include:

  • Time saved compared with the customer's previous approach
  • Reduction in errors or rework
  • Improvement in task completion
  • Reduction in operating costs
  • Increased productivity
  • Improvement in a relevant customer experience
  • Achievement of a specific business or personal goal

Where possible, record the customer's starting point before they begin using your solution.

This gives you something to compare against.

Be careful about attributing every improvement to your product. Other factors may influence the results.

docs.title: 3. Customer satisfaction and feedback
docs.text:
Quantitative metrics tell you what is happening. Customer conversations can help explain why.

Gather feedback about:

  • What customers find useful
  • What they find confusing or frustrating
  • Which problems remain unresolved
  • What prevents them from using the solution more often
  • What they would change
  • Whether they would continue using it

You can collect this information through interviews, short surveys, support conversations, and observations.

Don't rely exclusively on satisfaction ratings.

A participant may say they're satisfied while rarely using the product.

Compare what customers say with what they actually do.

docs.title: 4. Commercial viability
docs.text:
If your MVP or pilot involves a commercial offer, begin evaluating whether the business model could work.

Potential metrics include:

  • Paid conversion rate: The percentage of eligible prospects or participants who become paying customers.
  • Revenue: The money generated during the test.
  • Customer acquisition cost (CAC): The cost of acquiring a paying customer.
  • Cost to serve: The direct resources required to deliver and support the offering.
  • Gross margin: Revenue remaining after the applicable direct costs of delivering the product or service.
  • Renewal or continuation rate: The percentage of eligible customers who continue after the initial period.

Not every metric will be meaningful during a small pilot.

For example, CAC calculated from only a few customers may be highly unstable.

Focus on the information you can reliably collect and avoid drawing broad conclusions from limited data.

docs.title: Track the entire customer experience
docs.text:
Your test should help you understand what happens from the moment someone agrees to participate until the pilot ends.

Consider the following stages:

Recruitment

Are you reaching the right participants? What motivates them to join?

Onboarding

Can participants get started without unnecessary difficulty?

First use

Can they complete the main task and experience the intended value?

Ongoing use

Do they continue using the offering? What encourages or prevents them from returning?

Support

What questions, problems, or requests arise? How much effort does your team spend helping participants?

Completion or renewal

Do participants achieve the desired outcome? Do they want to continue using or paying for the solution?

Tracking the full experience can help you identify where customers encounter barriers.

For example, low usage may not mean customers don't value your solution.

It could mean onboarding is confusing, participants don't understand when to use it, or the product doesn't fit their existing workflow.

Investigate the cause before deciding what to change.

docs.title: Review results throughout the test
docs.text:
Don't wait until the pilot ends to evaluate what you've learned.

Schedule regular reviews to compare actual results with your expectations.

For a short pilot, a weekly review may be appropriate. Longer or more complex tests may require a different schedule.

During each review, ask:

  • Are participants using the solution as expected?
  • Are they experiencing the intended outcomes?
  • What problems or complaints have emerged?
  • Are there differences between customer segments?
  • What have we learned about adoption and willingness to pay?
  • Are our original assumptions still reasonable?
  • Do we need to change anything before continuing?

Review both numbers and customer feedback.

Look for patterns rather than reacting to every individual comment.

For small samples, examine individual customer experiences as well as averages. A few unusual results can significantly influence the overall numbers.

docs.title: Make improvements without losing track of what you're testing
docs.text:
You may discover problems that need to be fixed during your pilot.

Some changes, such as resolving a critical bug or addressing a safety issue, shouldn't wait until the test ends.

Other changes may be better scheduled between testing rounds.

Before making a significant change, record:

  • What problem prompted the change
  • What evidence supports it
  • What you're changing
  • When the change takes effect
  • Which participants will experience the new version
  • What result you expect

This helps you understand whether an improvement influenced the outcome.

For example, if you change your onboarding process halfway through a pilot, compare the experiences of participants who used the original process with those who used the updated version.

Don't assume that results collected under different conditions are directly comparable.

Improve the experience when needed, but keep a clear record of what was tested.

docs.title: Recognize when it's time to pivot
docs.text:
Not every MVP or pilot will support your original assumptions.

You may discover that customers don't experience enough value, that the solution is too difficult to adopt, or that a different group of customers responds more positively.

These findings may indicate that you need to change direction.

A pivot is a meaningful change to an important part of your business approach based on what you've learned.

A pivot doesn't necessarily mean abandoning your business idea.

It could involve changing:

  • Customer segment: Serving a different group of customers.
  • Customer problem: Focusing on a different need.
  • Solution: Using a different approach to address the problem.
  • Product scope: Making a different capability the centre of the offering.
  • Business model: Changing how customers pay or how the business generates revenue.
  • Distribution or acquisition channel: Reaching customers through a different approach.

For example, imagine you've developed a reporting tool for small retailers.

During testing, you discover that retailers rarely use it, but accounting firms working with those retailers find the reporting functionality valuable.

That finding might justify investigating accounting firms as a potential customer segment.

However, one unexpected conversation isn't enough to justify a major change.

Look for consistent evidence, investigate alternative explanations, and consider what additional testing could help you make the decision.

docs.title: Persevere, iterate, or pivot?
docs.text:
At the end of a testing round, consider three possible directions.

Persevere

Continue with your current approach when the evidence suggests that your target customers are receiving meaningful value and the business opportunity remains promising.

You may still need further validation before scaling.

Iterate

Improve your solution when the core problem and approach appear promising, but specific features, workflows, pricing, or processes need adjustment.

Pivot

Reconsider a fundamental assumption when repeated evidence suggests that your current approach is unlikely to deliver the intended value or support a viable business.

Sometimes the evidence is insufficient to choose confidently.

In that case, define the next experiment needed to resolve the uncertainty rather than forcing a decision.

docs.title: MVP/Pilot testing dashboard
docs.text:
Create a simple dashboard to track the metrics most relevant to your offering.

Category Metric Baseline Target Actual result Notes Participation Active participants Activation Participants completing the first meaningful action Usage Relevant usage frequency Customer value Main outcome achieved Experience Task completion or usability issues Commercial Paid conversions or revenue Operations Cost or effort to serve participants

You don't need to track every metric.

Choose a small set that helps you evaluate your most important assumptions.

Define each metric clearly so everyone involved understands how it's measured.

For example:

Activation rate = (Participants who complete the defined first meaningful action ÷ Eligible participants) × 100

Task completion rate = (Successfully completed task attempts ÷ Total valid task attempts) × 100

Paid conversion rate = (Participants who become paying customers ÷ Eligible participants offered a paid conversion) × 100

Use consistent definitions and time periods when comparing results.

docs.title: Assumption and experiment tracker
docs.text:
Use this tool to connect your original assumptions to the evidence collected during testing.

Assumption Test or observation Success criteria Actual evidence Decision Customers can complete the core task independently The solution improves their current process Participants will continue using the solution Customers will consider paying for the offering

Review the tracker throughout the pilot.

If an assumption isn't supported, investigate why before deciding what to change.

docs.title: Weekly pilot review
docs.text:
Use a recurring review to keep your team focused on learning and improvement.

1. Review the numbers

Compare actual results with your targets and previous observations.

2. Review customer feedback

Identify recurring problems, requests, and positive experiences.

3. Investigate differences

Explore why some participants are more successful or engaged than others.

4. Identify priorities

Choose the most important issues to address.

5. Assign actions

Record who is responsible for each next step and when it should happen.

6. Document decisions

Explain what you've decided, what evidence informed the decision, and what you expect to learn next.

Keep a record of each review so you can see how your understanding changes over time.

docs.title: Build-measure-learn loop
docs.text:
The Build-Measure-Learn framework is a way to improve a solution through repeated experiments.

It involves three connected activities:

  1. Build: Create or adjust the smallest offering or change needed to test an assumption.
  2. Measure: Observe how customers respond and collect relevant evidence.
  3. Learn: Decide what the evidence means and what to do next.

The process then repeats.

For example:

Build: Simplify your MVP's onboarding process.

Measure: Track whether new participants complete onboarding and reach the first meaningful action.

Learn: Determine whether the change improved activation or whether another barrier remains.

Use the framework to make purposeful changes rather than adding features without a clear reason.

docs.title: Pivot decision framework
docs.text:
Before making a significant change, summarize the evidence.

Question Your findings What assumption is being challenged? What evidence suggests it isn't holding up? How many relevant customers or situations support the finding? What alternative explanations have we considered? What new direction are we considering? What evidence supports that direction? What would we need to test next? What would it cost to continue versus change direction?

Use this framework to structure a discussion with your team or TechAlliance advisor.

A pivot should be a deliberate response to evidence, not simply a reaction to disappointing results.

docs.title: Google Sheets
docs.text:
Google Sheets can help you build a pilot dashboard, track participants, calculate metrics, and maintain an assumption and experiment tracker.

It can also help you compare results across different testing periods.

docs.title: Microsoft Excel
docs.text: Microsoft Excel can help you organize testing data, analyze results, and create charts showing changes in usage, customer outcomes, or operational performance.

docs.title: Google Forms
docs.text:
Google Forms can help you collect structured feedback from pilot participants.

Use short surveys at relevant points in the experience, such as after onboarding or at the end of the pilot.

Surveys should complement direct observations and usage data rather than replace them.

docs.title: PostHog
docs.text:
PostHog provides product analytics tools that can help digital product teams understand user behaviour.

Depending on your implementation, you may be able to track events such as onboarding completion, feature usage, and customer journeys.

Define the behaviours you need to measure before implementing analytics.

Configure data collection with appropriate privacy, consent, and security considerations.

docs.title: Microsoft Clarity
docs.text:
Microsoft Clarity provides tools for understanding how people interact with websites, including heatmaps and session recordings.

It may help you identify usability issues and areas where users encounter difficulty.

Review privacy requirements and configure the tool appropriately before collecting visitor interaction data.

docs.title: Trello
docs.text:
Trello can help you manage issues, improvement requests, and tasks that emerge during testing.

Create a simple workflow for recording, prioritizing, assigning, and completing changes.

docs.title: Put it into practice
docs.text:
Manage an MVP or pilot testing round from start to finish.

Your goal is to collect enough relevant evidence to make an informed decision about your solution and the next steps for your business.

Start by reviewing your MVP/Pilot definition and solution interview findings.

Then:

  1. Confirm your assumptions. Identify the most important things you need to validate about customer value, usability, adoption, and commercial potential.
  2. Choose your metrics. Select a small set of indicators directly connected to those assumptions.
  3. Record your baseline. Document how customers currently address the problem and what outcomes they experience, where measurable.
  4. Prepare the test. Confirm participants, responsibilities, timelines, onboarding, support, and relevant safeguards.
  5. Launch the MVP or pilot. Give participants access to the offering and explain what they can expect.
  6. Monitor activity. Track usage, customer outcomes, support needs, and any operational problems.
  7. Collect feedback. Speak with participants regularly to understand what is and isn't working.
  8. Review results. Hold periodic reviews to compare evidence with your expectations.
  9. Document changes. Record improvements made during the test and their potential effects.
  10. Make a decision. Determine whether to persevere, iterate, pivot, or conduct another focused experiment.

At the end of the test, prepare a short summary covering:

  • What you intended to validate
  • Who participated and how the test was conducted
  • What you measured
  • What actually happened
  • What customers said and did
  • Which assumptions were supported or challenged
  • What changes were made during the test
  • What you recommend doing next

Before making your next decision, ask yourself:

  • Did the solution address the problem we intended to solve?
  • Did participants experience measurable value?
  • Did they use the solution as expected?
  • What prevented some participants from adopting or continuing to use it?
  • Did we learn anything meaningful about willingness to pay?
  • Can we deliver the offering reliably and at a reasonable cost?
  • Which assumptions remain uncertain?
  • Do the results support continuing, improving, or changing our approach?
  • What is the most important thing we need to test next?

Consider reviewing your results with your TechAlliance advisor before committing significant resources to further development or growth.

Remember: Validation isn't about proving that your original idea was right.

It's about gathering evidence, learning from real customer behaviour, and making informed decisions about what to build, improve, or change.

The strongest outcome of an MVP or pilot is a clearer understanding of whether your solution creates meaningful customer value and what your business should do next.

docs.title: Turn your research into an offer you can test
docs.text:
You've spent time understanding your potential customers, investigating their problems, speaking with subject-matter experts, and exploring how your business might address those needs.

Now it's time to define what you'll actually offer your first users or customers.

During the Discovery stage, you developed an initial product roadmap and go-to-market (GTM) plan. These documents helped you identify the problems worth addressing, the customers you want to reach, and the outcomes your proposed solution should deliver.

The Validation stage is where you begin testing whether your solution works for those customers.

An MVP (minimum viable product) is the smallest usable version of your product that delivers meaningful value while allowing you to test important assumptions.

A pilot is a limited trial of your product or service with a defined group of participants, scope, and timeframe.

An MVP and a pilot aren't the same thing, but they can work together. For example, you might develop an MVP and invite a small group of customers to use it during a four-week pilot.

Your goal is to define:

  • What you're offering: The product, service, or experience participants will receive.
  • Who it's for: The specific customers or users you want to test it with.
  • What's included: The essential features, services, or activities available during the test.
  • What's excluded: The capabilities or improvements you'll leave for later.
  • How participation works: The number of participants, duration, onboarding, and support.
  • What participants will pay: Whether the offer is free, discounted, or paid.
  • What success looks like: The evidence you'll collect to decide what to do next.

An MVP or pilot isn't about launching an unfinished version of everything you hope to build. It's about offering something focused enough to test, but useful enough to create real value.

docs.title: Start with the problem you've validated
docs.text:
Before defining your MVP or pilot, return to your customer discovery findings.

Ask yourself:

  • Which customer problem appeared most important?
  • Who experienced it most frequently or intensely?
  • What are customers doing to solve it today?
  • What outcomes are they trying to achieve?
  • Which assumptions about the problem are supported by evidence?
  • What did subject-matter experts identify as important constraints?

Your initial offer should address a specific problem for a specific group of people.

For example, imagine you've interviewed small business owners who spend several hours each week manually preparing reports.

Your long-term product vision might include automated reporting, dashboards, forecasting, integrations, and AI-generated recommendations.

But your first MVP might focus only on helping users combine information from two sources and generate one useful report.

This gives you a clearer opportunity to test whether your approach solves a meaningful problem.

docs.title: Decide whether you need an MVP, a pilot, or both
docs.text:
The right approach depends on your business model, solution, and what you need to learn.

An MVP is useful when you need a working version of your proposed solution that customers can interact with.

For example:

  • A software startup releases a basic application with one essential workflow.
  • A marketplace tests a limited service in one geographic area.
  • A consumer product company offers a simplified first version of its product.

A pilot is useful when you want to test an offering under defined conditions with selected participants.

For example:

  • A B2B startup works with three organizations to test a new workflow.
  • A service business delivers a four-week program to a small group of clients.
  • A technology company installs a solution at one customer site to assess its performance.

A pilot may use an MVP, an existing product, or a service delivered partly through manual processes.

In some cases, a prototype, demonstration, or other experiment may be more appropriate before investing in a fully usable MVP.

Choose the smallest approach that can produce meaningful evidence while meeting the safety, quality, privacy, and other requirements relevant to your offering.

docs.title: Define exactly what you're offering
docs.text:
Your MVP or pilot should have a clear scope.

Start by describing the experience from the participant's perspective.

What will they receive? What will they be able to accomplish? What will your team provide?

For example:

"We'll offer a four-week pilot to five independent retailers. Participants will use a basic inventory reporting tool to consolidate sales information from two sources. We'll provide onboarding and weekly support, and we'll collect feedback on usability and time spent preparing reports."

This is more useful than saying:

"We're launching an inventory management platform."

The first statement explains the target customer, the offer, its boundaries, and how the pilot will operate.

Be clear about any limitations so participants know what to expect.

docs.title: Select the features that matter most
docs.text:
Your product roadmap may contain many opportunities and possible features.

You don't need to include all of them in your MVP.

Start with the features or activities required to deliver the core value you're trying to test.

For each proposed feature, ask:

  • Does it directly address the customer problem?
  • Is it necessary for the user to complete the main task?
  • Will it help us test an important assumption?
  • Is there a simpler way to deliver the same value?
  • Can we postpone it without undermining the test?

Distinguish between:

  • Essential features: Required to deliver the core experience and test your main assumptions.
  • Supporting features: Useful, but not necessary for the first version.
  • Future features: Potential improvements that can wait until you've collected feedback.

Don't remove features or safeguards that are necessary for safety, accessibility, reliability, privacy, security, or regulatory compliance simply to make the MVP smaller.

Minimum viable means the smallest version that can deliver and test value responsibly, not the cheapest version you can release.

docs.title: Choose your first users or customers
docs.text:
Your initial participants should reflect the customer segment you've identified through Discovery.

Return to your customer segmentation research and Customer Zoom Tool.

Look for people who:

  • Experience the problem you're addressing
  • Match the characteristics of your intended customer segment
  • Can realistically use or evaluate your offering
  • Are willing to participate under clearly explained conditions
  • Can provide relevant feedback or evidence about the solution

For B2B businesses, consider whether you need to involve end users, purchasing decision-makers, or both.

For B2C businesses, consider the behaviours and circumstances that make someone an appropriate early participant.

How many participants do you need?

There isn't one number that works for every MVP or pilot.

The right number depends on what you're testing, the variability among users, your available resources, and how much evidence you need.

A small initial pilot may be useful for observing workflows and identifying usability problems. It won't necessarily provide enough evidence to estimate market-wide demand or customer retention.

Choose a participant target you can explain, and be clear about the limits of what your results will demonstrate.

docs.title: Decide whether to charge for your pilot
docs.text:
One of the most important decisions is whether participants will pay to use your MVP or take part in your pilot.

There's no universal answer.

The right approach depends on your business model, what you're offering, and what you need to validate.

docs.title: Free pilot
docs.text:
A free pilot may make sense when:

  • You're primarily testing usability or technical performance.
  • The solution is still experimental.
  • Participation requires significant feedback or collaboration.
  • You need to reduce barriers to initial participation.

However, willingness to use something for free doesn't demonstrate willingness to pay.

If you choose a free pilot, plan how you'll investigate pricing and purchasing behaviour later.

docs.title: Discounted pilot
docs.text:
A discounted pilot may help you:

  • Reduce the financial commitment for early customers.
  • Test whether customers are willing to pay something.
  • Recognize that participants are accepting limitations or contributing feedback.

Be clear about the regular price you expect to charge, if known, and what happens when the pilot ends.

docs.title: Paid pilot
docs.text:
A paid pilot may be appropriate when:

  • The offering already delivers meaningful value.
  • Customers recognize the problem and have a reason to address it.
  • You're ready to test a commercial relationship.
  • The scope, price, responsibilities, and expectations can be clearly defined.

A paid pilot can provide stronger evidence of willingness to pay than positive feedback alone.

However, payment by a small number of early customers doesn't automatically establish that your pricing or business model will work at scale.

Whatever approach you choose, explain the terms clearly before participation begins.

docs.title: Set a timeframe and participant expectations
docs.text:
A pilot should have a defined beginning and end.

Your timeline should provide enough opportunity for participants to experience the offering and for your team to collect useful evidence.

Consider:

  • How long does onboarding take?
  • How frequently will participants use the product or service?
  • How much time is needed to observe meaningful results?
  • When will you collect feedback?
  • What support will your team provide?
  • What happens when the pilot ends?

For example, a four-week pilot might include an onboarding session, three weeks of use, and a final feedback conversation.

That timeline may work for some products but not for others.

A solution used once a year will require a different testing approach from a tool used every day.
